Railway Act Amendment

subtopic: APPLICATION OF MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND

speechtext:
The house resumed from April 26 consideration in committee of Bill No. 220 to amend the Railway Act-Mr. Dunning-Mr. Marcil in the chair.
On Section 1-Railway grade crossing fund.

subtopic: APPLICATION OF MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
We were still on section
1 when the house adjourned last night, Mr. Chairman. I think probably the discussion had proceeded not as far as the members of the committee desired. I shall be glad to deal with any further questions which may arise.

subtopic: APPLICATION OF MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: Does this bill contain any provision that would debar small towns or municipalities from making applications in the future for railway crossings?

subtopic: APPLICATION OF MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: Absolutely no. The intention of the amending bill is, as I explained last night, entirely in the opposite direction. There is certainly no greater restriction; on the contrary there is greater freedom to make application.

subtopic: APPLICATION OF MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
Is it the intention that this
should apply to maintenance as well as construction in the first instance?

subtopic: APPLICATION OF MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
The section reads "not
including that of maintenance."

subtopic: APPLICATION OF MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: This situation sometimes arises: there is a separation of grades, and perhaps under the terms of the agreement between the municipality and the railway company an overhead bridge is constructed. Twenty years later-as in the case I have in mind-it may be necessary to make substantial repairs. Why should there not be some allowance out of the fund to take care of such a situation? In the case to which I am referring the municipality is paying 50 per cent and the railway 50 per cent of the cost of separation. It seems to me that that would be an appropriate case for, say, a 40 per cent allowance from this fund, the balance to be borne equally by the railway and the municipality. If the legislation does not so apply-and I may say frankly that I understand it does not-does not the 'minister 'think it is a matter that might well receive consideration? I have thought the matter over, and I can see no reason why the fund should not apply to such a case.

subtopic: APPLICATION OF MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
As I intimated last night, I want to make more elastic the conditions under which the grade crossing fund is ad-
56103- 155
ministered, in order to widen the use for which it was created. I would direct the hon. gentleman's attention to the fact that grade separation is the real object in view. As long as there are so many thousands of dangerous crossings throughout the country to be dealt with, I am afraid that to so change the law as to make it apply to maintenance as well as construction would be going too far, having regard to the amount which parliament is annually voting for the fund at the present time. However, I should like to call attention to this:	It is evident
from the history of the fund that more than one contribution has been ordered with respect to the same crossing. Out of 520 crossings dealt with since the inception of the grade crossing fund, some 44 have been dealt with by more than one grant. I am advised that that second grant does not in any sense involve what my hon. friend has just pointed out, repairs to an existing structure, but rather a change in the character of the protection afforded. That is to say, there might be in the first place a wig-wag, for which ten years later gates might be substituted. I believe both the present statute and the amending bill would permit that.

subtopic: APPLICATION OF MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: That is really construction.

subtopic: APPLICATION OF MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: That is really construction, but I do not believe that either the present act or the amending bill would permit maintenance charges, such as replanking a bridge, and so forth, to be entertained. Much as I sympathize with the position outlined by my hon. friend, I suggest we had better not widen the legislation to that extent. If the municipality is fortunate enough to have received, together with the railway company, a contribution to the extent of 40 per cent of the original cost, it is not so much of a burden to keep the structure in reasonable repair.

subtopic: APPLICATION OF MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
Unfortunately that is not so
in the case I have in mind, because the bridge in question was constructed before this fund was available. There has been no contribution whatever in connection with the construction, but it was thought proper, having in view the public safety, that the grade should be separated. It was separated and now the time for repair has arisen. Naturally therefore I was anxious to have the fund made applicable to a case o/ that kind. I can understand however that if it is not applicable to maintenance in any case it cculd not be made applicable here even if there was no allowance originally made for construction.

Railway Act Amendment

subtopic: APPLICATION OF MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
Is there any provision
for the deviation of a road to avoid a railway crossing altogether? I have in mind the approach to a town in my riding. Parry Sound, where there are seven crossings within a very short distance, all dangerous. I believe that if this act provided for a case of that kind a deviation could be made to avoid most of the crossings.

subtopic: APPLICATION OF MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
In the past, as I
explained last evening, the fund has been used for the purpose of diversion, such as my hon. friend refers to, and the definitions contained in this amending section in no way alter that condition. In this section "crossing" means any railway crossing on a highway, or any highway crossing on a railway at rail level, and every manner of construction of the railway or of the highway, by elevation or depression of the one above or below the other, or by diversion of one or the other, and so forth.

subtopic: APPLICATION OF MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: That is all right.

Section agreed to.
Section 2 agreed to.
On the preamble.

subtopic: APPLICATION OF MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: I understand the proportion contributed by the Dominion is 40 per cent.

subtopic: APPLICATION OF MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
Not exceeding 40 per
cent.

subtopic: APPLICATION OF MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: In any case where there might be two or three high bridges, or viaducts, required, and a deviation of the road might eliminate this necessity, would the minister be prepared to say that they should then limit themselves to 40 per cent on the deviation?

subtopic: APPLICATION OF MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
That raises a question
which has occurred more or less frequently under the existing law, for the reason that there was a limitation on the number of crossings within one municipality to which the board might apply the funds in any one year. But that limitation has been removed. There is somewhere provision for the declaration by the board that the work is one work of safety. I cannot put my finger on the exact phraseology, but if my hon. friend will read the bill he will find somewhere that it is provided that any work may be declared by the board' to be a single work of protection.

subtopic: APPLICATION OF MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
The point I am trying
to make is that a deviation might obviate three or four crossings.
[Mr. Boys.l

subtopic: APPLICATION OF MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: Yes, so long as the work is declared to be one work.

subtopic: APPLICATION OF MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: Will the bill make it compulsory for a municipality to make alterations intended in this legislation?

subtopic: APPLICATION OF MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
There is no compulsion
involved in the bill. The power of the board remains exactly the same in that regard as it is to-day.

subtopic: APPLICATION OF MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: How are the proportions arrived at which are contributed respectively by the municipality, the province and the railways? Is it by agreement?

subtopic: APPLICATION OF MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: That is within the judgment of the Board of Railway Commissioners, and dependent upon the circumstances of the particular case, having regard to the date at which the crossing came into existence and having regard also to which is senior, the railway or the highway. Many considerations are involved and they vary in particular cases. It is not possible to read through the board's rulings in various cases and arrive at anything which may be -said to be an absolutely fixed principle applicable in all cases. This is one of the matters which the board must analyse in relation to the circumstances surrounding the particular crossing under review.

subtopic: APPLICATION OF MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: It is subject to the railway board?

subtopic: APPLICATION OF MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: APPLICATION OF MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
Does not the minister
think that there should be some rule established whereby, when the highway is senior to the railway, the railway company should be required to pay the whole cost of providing protection at the crossing, subject of course to any allowance being made out of the fund?

subtopic: APPLICATION OF MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
That point was dealt
with last evening, and I can only refer my hon. friend to section 260 of the act. In any case where a railway has been constructed after the nineteenth day of May, 1909, the railway company shall at its own cost and expense, unless as otherwise provided by agreement, approved by the board, between the company and the municipal or other corporation or person, provide, subject to the order of the board, protection, safety and convenience for the public in crossing a highway by a railway. That is to say, in respect of ail crossings which came into existence since 1909, the railway company is prima facie responsible for the protection there required. This is subject to exceptions, such for example as where a roadway was in existence on paper in 1909-that is to say, it was dedicated as a roadway-

Railway Act Amendment

subtopic: APPLICATION OF MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: A road allowance.

subtopic: APPLICATION OF MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
Yes, a road allowance,
as we call it in- the west. In a subsequent year that road allowance is used and the railway company makes representations to the board that traffic has arisen in connection with that particular crossing which was not there and not contemplated when the railway was built. In such cases the board has not rigidly applied the rule that the railway must pay. The other rule then comes into operation, as to which is senior in point of fact and of operation. Another difficulty which I find in some cases, regardless of the time oi construction of the crossing, is where the need for protection arises by reason of increased traffic over either the highway or the railway. In many instances the need arises through increased railway traffic not comtem-plated when the crossing was instituted.

subtopic: APPLICATION OF MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
Broad street at Regina,
for instance.

subtopic: APPLICATION OF MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
Yes, Broad street at
Regma is an excellent instance in point. It was increased traffic on the railway in that case which made necessary the work of protection, and in consequence the railway had to pay very much more than the proportion it would otherwise have been called upon to contribute. Then you have the possible case where the railway traffic remains substantially the same but where the highway traffic, due to the building, let us say, of a trunk highway, has increased materially.

subtopic: APPLICATION OF MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: As at Albert street, west of Regina.

subtopic: APPLICATION OF MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
Yes, that would be an
instance. In that case the railway board takes into account the relations between the parties and adjudicates. In general I think it may be said that the administration by the Board of Railway Commissioners, under its successive chairmen, of this particular section of the law, has been about as satisfactory as such a piece of legislation in operation could be. My hon. friend from New Westminster (Mr. McQuarrie) suggests some general rule.
I can assure him that if he reads through the acts and gets an idea of the very varied circumstances which obtain between crossings in different parts of Canada, he will find it as difficult as I do to attempt to apply any rigid general rule.

subtopic: APPLICATION OF MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
I have read through
the cases, and in fact have taken part in some of them. I have found that generally the board will say, "Well, yes, we will give you the protection at this crossing but you
56103-155J
will have to share the cost equally with the railway or you will have to pay all the expenses." That happens even when the highway is senior to the railway by a number of years, and it seems to me that'some provision should be made whereby the board cannot give a ruling of that kind. I will admit that the Board of Railway Commissioners is an impartial body and tries to do its best, but at the same time it has come to be pretty much a board which stands for the protection of the railway companies, as far as I can see, more than for the protection of the public as it used to be. Consequently I suggest that the minister might consider the advisability of bringing in some legislation which would cover the matter in so many words, in order to leave no discretion to the Board of Railway Commissioners in dealing with that particular subject.

subtopic: APPLICATION OF MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
I am afraid I cannot
make my friend that promise; my study of this matter convinces me that such positiveness would tend to make an already difficult situation rather worse. Of course I appreciate the fact that in cases before the board the party who does not succeed is like the unsuccessful party in an ordinary lawsuit; usually he is not satisfied, and that is equally true of the railway companies. They have come to me and pointed out where grave injustices have been done to them in certain cases, but after balancing things up I think the board has administered this measure about as well as we could expect it to be looked after,

subtopic: APPLICATION OF MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
If they slowed down
the trains at crossings it would be an entirely different matter, but as a general rule they do not do so. They go across the highways at a rather excessive speed in many cases, and that is where the difficulty arises. Possibly they could be compelled to moderate their speed if the matter were taken to court, but that is always a hazardous proceeding. As a general rule the danger exists because the railway operates trains along tracks which cross highways; the danger does not come from pedestrians or motorists running into trains.

subtopic: APPLICATION OF MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
Last night I gave the
figures for last year; seventy-four motor cars ran into the sides of moving trains.

subtopic: APPLICATION OF MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
Why did they do that? The trains must have been going too fast. That is the very point, but in any event it seems to me that the lives of motorists and pedestrians should be taken care of at these crossings to a greater extent than is the case at present. I know it is absolutely impossible
Railway Act Amendment

to prevent some of these motorists from getting into accidents; I quite appreciate that fact, but the way it appeals to me is that the crossing is dangerous because of the operation of the railway trains. Therefore the railway companies should be compelled to provide the necessary signals and to take the necessary precautions to minimize the number of accidents in cases where the highway is senior to the railway.
Mr. ARTHUR,S: The minister has informed the house that in connection with crossings constructed before 1909 the onus is upon the railway to provide the protection necessary for the safety of the public. I believe I am right in that?

subtopic: APPLICATION OF MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: Subject to the exception which I read.

subtopic: APPLICATION OF MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
As a general principle
that is true. On the other hand, the present act allows the Board of Railway Commissioners to give 40 per cent of the cost of improving the protection at railway crossings, and no more than 40 per cent.

subtopic: APPLICATION OF MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: That does not apply to crossings constructed since 1909.

subtopic: APPLICATION OF MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: I am not referring to those at the moment. I would like to ask the minister whether a deviation would be allowed for, and to what extent, by his department. In my riding I have a municipality which contains seven railway crossings within a distance of about three miles, all built subsequent to the highway which they cross. Manifestly it would be impossible for a small municipality to pay even 40 per cent of the cost of protecting those seven crossings.

subtopic: APPLICATION OF MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: The highway was there first?

subtopic: APPLICATION OF MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: Yes, and I would suggest that the act be broadened out to take care of special cases of this kind where a railway, through the agency of its surveyors, has crossed a highway repeatedly within a very short distance. To some extent the municipality should be assisted in a special way.

subtopic: APPLICATION OF MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: I will not presume to give legal advice, but I am reasonably sure that such eases are already within the competence of the railway board. I am satisfied that that is the law, subject to the opinions of my legal friends.

subtopic: APPLICATION OF MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
I would like to ask the minister a question, and I hope he will pardon me for doing so, because probably I *should know all about it. However, I have not had time to study this bill. I understand .that the grant is $200,000 a year?
{Mr. McQuarrie.]

subtopic: APPLICATION OF MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: APPLICATION OF MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: Will that be sufficient to take care of the applications?

subtopic: APPLICATION OF MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
No; I would hope not.
I will explain that to my hon. friend when he finishes his question.

subtopic: APPLICATION OF MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: The point I wish to make is that we should enlarge the grant so that these death-traps throughout the country might be eliminated as quickly as possible, having in view the rapid increase in motor traffic.

subtopic: APPLICATION OF MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
Perhaps I should have gone more fully over the discussion which took place last evening. The fact is that the fund has not been expended. In practice the provisions of the law have not proven sufficiently elastic for those interested to avail themselves of the assistance granted, with the result that there is still in the fund over $600,000 which was placed there prior to 1919 as earmarked money. In addition to that there is available, under statute, the accumulation of $200,000 for each year since 1919, making a total of about $2,600,000 available to the board. So we are in this position: Under the provisions of the law as it has existed we have only succeeded in spending about $1,300,000 in eighteen years, whereas parliament has provided $3,800,000 during that period. The whole object of this amending legislation, with its increase in the maximum from $25,000 to $100,000 for an individual crossing and the other loosening provisions, if I might so term them, is to make it possible for the fund to be used more generally for the purpose for which it was assigned. I might point out further to my hon. friend that in respect of the annual appropriation by parliament, under the original legislation of 1909 the annual statutory contribution of $200,000 applied for ten years. In 1919 that statutory appropriation was renewed for a further ten years, which means that it will expire in 1929. I am not in this bill proposing any extension of that, in the hope that during the year which is coming we shall get experience of the working of these amendments and have thereby a better idea of what to propose to parliament with respect to future grants. I may say that I do not hope, as I explained last night, that the grade crossing fund in anything like the proporions financially which we contribute to it annually will eliminate the level crossing difficulty in Canada. We must recognize that every level crossing of a highway by a railway or vice versa is a place where a fatality is liable to occur sooner or later.

Railway Act Amendment

subtopic: APPLICATION OF MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
How many thousands
are there?

subtopic: APPLICATION OF MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
Tens of thousands of
level crossings. I mentioned last night that in the United States some of the states are to-day spending up to hundreds of millions in protection and grade separation work, in cooperation with the railways; and it has been freely stated before the Interstate Commerce Commission that to apply rigidly the law as it exists in that country with respect to protection and grade separation would bankrupt the railways of the United States; that is to apply literally the true spirt of the law in forcing grade separation generally in every case. It has become an increasing problem, and of course the railways take the ground that the problem has assumed its more serious aspect largely on account of the development of another type of traffic which in fact competes with the railways and has the effect of reducing their revenues. For instance, my hon. friend from New Westminster (Mr. Mc-Quarrie) suggested a minute ago that railway trains might slow up when approaching a crossing and make crossings more safe. But looking at the competition which is against them, it would mean that they would slow up in competition wth the trucks, making themselves more subject to competiton by backing down as it were in favour of their competitors.
I do not pretend for a moment that the amendments before the house will remedy anything; really the fund is intended as an inducement to those parties who are interested, municipalities, provinces and railways, to deal with the question, the inducement being a contribution from a fund provided by the federal treasury for the purpose. Up to the present, as I have said, it has not been made use of to the extent desired, and these provisions are introduced with the idea of creating a greater utility

subtopic: APPLICATION OF MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I am glad to hear the minister say that he wishes this accumulated fund to be used, and that these amendments have been introduced to make it more available. To my mind however it has accumulated largely because of the action of the Board of Railway Commissioners.

subtopic: APPLICATION OF MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: That is true.

subtopic: APPLICATION OF MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
If they
had been a little more lenient in their rulings in regard to grade crossings, I think this fund would have been entirely used up and perhaps more would have been required. To my mind we may amend this present act, pass
these amendments which I think are all right, but we will still have a deterrent in the Board of Railway Commissioners and this fund will not be made available as it should be. I cited a case last evening of a crossing on a provincial highway in the province of Ontario, one of the most densely travelled roads in the province.

subtopic: APPLICATION OF MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
Which was senior, the
railway or the highway?

subtopic: APPLICATION OF MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: The highway was senior. There a grade crossing is still maintained, with a wigwag and a bell, whereas the local municipality really wanted a subway. I think it might not be out of the way for this house to take into consideration at some time that at least on our provincial highways we should have separated crossings, either subways or overhead bridges, especially on the main tourist roads and over the main lines of railways. Then something should be done to induce the Board of Railway Commissioners to be a little more lenient in their rulings in regard to these grade crossings; if that were brought about this fund would be used up.

subtopic: APPLICATION OF MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
I confess I am not able
to understand why the application in the case mentioned by the hon. member for Lambton should not have been acceded to. When he says the highway was senior to the railway, it is even less capable of being explained. I fancy the minister is much in the same position as I am in respect to the reason for it. I only recall one case after this fund was first made available in which I heard an order made by the board that a portion of the cost of the separation of the grades should be borne out of this fund.
The whole effect of this act probably is to enable two or three communities to deal with a situation with which otherwise they could not deal; and in addition we have enabled the fund possibly between now and May, 1929, to be used to an extent that it has not been used. Knowing how earnest and zealous the hon. member for Lambton is for his constituency, I have no doubt that his municipality will make an early application to the board. I am sure that this house will be very interested in learning why the municipality controlling the highway, being senior, is not given relief. The real fact is that the lawyers for the railways have succeeded in inducing the board to believe that the present protection is adequate.

subtopic: APPLICATION OF MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
That is about the story, on the facts, as we hear them in the house.
Railway Act Amendment

subtopic: APPLICATION OF MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: May I ask the minister is this applicable to any crossing, or are there any restrictions?

subtopic: APPLICATION OF MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: No restrictions.

subtopic: APPLICATION OF MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: There are no restrictions.

subtopic: APPLICATION OF MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I
must admit that in this bill the minister has gone pretty far, but he has not yet gone far enough to look after the wishes of the public. A too great economy will operate adversely to the public interest. It will not save one life in the Dominion of Canada. They have first a little bell, then a light, and then a light a hundred yards or so away from the crossing; and then the next thing will be that perhaps the light will be extended a hundred yards further; and that is all that will be done. As I said last night, there is only one solution of this problem, and that is to get away from the grade crossing; there is no way in this bill to secure the safety of the public. I quite admit that there are cases where the public are to blame; but there is the crossing and there is the danger light, and not only can a reckless driver risk his own life but, on the way, he picks up one or two innocent passengers who are very often sacrificed. The minister or somebody should go another step further and say that where more than one accident has happened grade separation must follow. On these highways they have had not only accidents once a year but once a month, and some drastic action should be taken.

subtopic: APPLICATION OF MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: What drastic action?

subtopic: APPLICATION OF MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: Force a bridge or an underground passageway.

subtopic: APPLICATION OF MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
APPLICATION OF MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: The minister must admit that I used the word "highway". I was not referring to these little feeders.

subtopic: APPLICATION OF MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
I am afraid I have not made myself clear. I was referring to branch

line railways which are crossed by a main highway, where there is plenty of highway traffic but an infrequent train service. In fact railway men tell me that they are more subject to crossing accidents at a crossing on a railroad which is not very often used by trains than they are in cases where the trains are running with considerable regularity. The reason for that is that people become accustomed to speeding across such a crossing; they say: It is only a branch line; there i3 no train to-day or no train this week. That is how a great number of the accidents occur and the adoption of any fixed rule seems to be impossible. I am sure the Board of Railway Commissioners will take cognizance not only of this legislation but of the expressions of view by hon. members with respect to the spirit in which we desire this legislation to be administered. Much as I desire to lay down some fixed rule, I find some objection such as that which I have just mentioned, to every suggestion which comes forward along that line.

subtopic: APPLICATION OF MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
I should like to suggest
to the minister that in addition to protecting the public against railways built since 1909, we should have a differential in favour of a municipality where a railway has a crossing which is obstructed either by nature or in some other way, and it is difficult for the public to have a view of the railway either to the right or to the left.

subtopic: APPLICATION OF MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: That was also dealt with last night. Section 258 of the present act gives the railway commission the fullest possible power in relation to anything of any nature which obstructs the view.

subtopic: APPLICATION OF MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
Only up to forty per
cent of the liability.

subtopic: APPLICATION OF MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
The grade fund is not
usable with respect to the removal of obstructions of view. It is only available with respect to the construction of the actual work of protecting the crossing. But the board has very full and wide powers with respect to the removal of any obstruction to the view of a person approaching the crossing, no matter what the cause of the obstruction of view may be.

subtopic: APPLICATION OF MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
Where a railway has not only its main track but sidings across a highway close to a town and a dangerous condition exists, is there legislation to compel the railway to provide protection at such places? In my town there are four crossings [DOT]within a mile and on every one of them a number of people have been killed.

Railway Act Amendment
Within the last five or six years at least eight people have been killed on those four crossings and yet nothing has been done either by the municipality or by the railway to protect the public.

subtopic: APPLICATION OF MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: There is no compulsion on anybody. The Railway Act provides the machinery through which anyone interested may take action, but it in no way compels any of the bodies concerned to act, that is by way of motion. There is, of course, machinery whereby the railway commission can compel the railway company to do such and such. As regards the initiation of the motion to bring about some protection, surely in a case such as that referred to by my hon. friend there must be sufficient people interested in the municipality concerned to ensure that the municipality would apply to the board for whatever protection they deemed necessary in the circumstances. If there is not that, I am afraid there is in the law nothing which would compel them so to do.

subtopic: APPLICATION OF MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: On more than one occasion a conference has been had between the municipality and the railway company but there seems to be no provision by which any of these improvements can be enforced. Apparently it is entirely a question of two or three people who are interested coming to some agreement and as a consequence nothing has ever been done. I know on two occasions there have been conferences between the municipality of the town or the township and the railway, and yet nothing has come of them.

subtopic: APPLICATION OF MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
While a friendly conference is of course always desirable preceding any attempt at litigation-and as a matter of fact an application to the board is litigation-there is provision in the law for bringing a matter of this kind to the attention of the board. Section 257 of the present Railway Act reads:
Where a railway is already constructed upon, along or across any highway, the board may of its own motion, or upon complaint or application, by or on behalf of the crown, or any municipal or other corporation, or any person aggrieved, order the company to submit to the board, within a specified time, a plan-
And so forth. There is the widest kind of provision for application to the commission. In fact under that section my hon. friend could himself make an application to the board with respect to those dangerous crossings.

subtopic: APPLICATION OF MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
In fact the section that the minister has just read was inserted to meet the very situation to which the hon.
member for Halton has referred. It used to be that no one except the municipality and the railway might deal with these matters, and if my memory serves me aright the board when Mr. Justice Mabee was chairman, instructed their engineers, whenever reports of accidents came to them, to see what action should be taken. From that there was an extension of the power and it is not infrequently that members of parliament write to the board asking them to make an inspection and to see what action may be taken to protect human life at dangerous crossings. I know that because of my experience in another capacity something over ten year ago. The whole purpose for which this money was voted by parliament was to meet cases where municipalities and railways could not agree and where it would be too great a hardship to ask the municipality to do all the work. It was to cover the cost up to forty per cent so that in some cases the burden was only ten per cent on the municipality, fifty per cent on the railway and the remaining forty per cent was taken out of this fund.

subtopic: APPLICATION OF MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: In view of the fact that economy seems to control the application of the remedy to this level crossing problem, does the minister not think it advisable to make provision that a larger proportion of the cost be defrayed out of this fund?

subtopic: APPLICATION OF MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
That is what the bill
provides.

subtopic: APPLICATION OF MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: What proportion?

subtopic: APPLICATION OF MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: The provision in the existing law is forty per cent with a maximum of 125,000. The provision in this bill is forty per cent in cases where the work to be done costs less than 8100,000, and forty per cent with a limit of 8100.000 in all cases where the cost exceeds S100,000. It is a quadrupling of the possible contribution in the particular case.

subtopic: APPLICATION OF MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: Would the minister consider, where the cost is less than $100,000, increasing the contribution from forty per cent to fifty, sixty, or seventy per cent? The fund is accumulating; we are not spending it, and people are being killed. My point is that we should get some action. At the rate we are going, it will be the middle of eternity before anything worth while is done.

subtopic: APPLICATION OF MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
I can best answer my hon. friend by referring him to the leader of the opposition, who very wisely said, in his first remarks' upon this subject yesterday, that the objective of the grade crossing fund was not the giving of large sums by way of federal assistance to large works, but rather
Railway Act Amendment

the providing of works of protection of one kind or another in the great number of cases throughout the country that are outside the cities altogether. I am already increasing the limit, and if the percentage were to be increased, that would, of course, tend still further to segregate the expenditure out of this fund to the larger works in the larger centres, and I arrived at the conclusion to retain the forty per cent in its relation to $100,000 as it previously existed in relation to $25,000, as being a pretty substanial step forward which would result in the fund being used to a greater extent. I think my hon. friend might consent to allow this to be tried for one year, so that we may see to what, extent the fund will be depleted. I am reasonably sure that it will go down very rapidly.

subtopic: APPLICATION OF MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: There will be no money left next year.

subtopic: APPLICATION OF MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: Not after we apply the provisions of this legislation.

subtopic: APPLICATION OF MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: What I had in mind was that the percentage might be greater than 40 per cent, say 50 or 70 per cent, in the case of works where the cost was comparatively small, not exceeding perhaps $25,000. I am not referring to crossings in town'., but out on the main highways.

Section agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time, and passed.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH

speechtext:
Hon. J. H. KING (Minister of Health) moved the second reading of Bill No. 205, respecting the Departments of Health and Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the house went into committee theron, Mr. Marcil in the chair.
On section 1-Short title.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
The minister will recall
that the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Clark) and some of his associates who are absent from the city are greatly interested in the question of the name, and possibly the minister would not object if later on they might make their suggestions as to the name during the further progress of the bill through the house, and that it will not be taken that we have finally disposed of section 1. I have no desire to delay the legislation, but I should like to reserve that right for them.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Since the resolution was under discussion, it was decided to leave the question of the name until we came into committee, but I have since had consultations with various people who are interested in the title of the department. I am most anxious that all should be satisfied, but, of course, there may still be disagreement. I think, however, that the proposed title, "The Department of Pensions and National Health" will properly designate the activities of the department, and what I would suggest is that we pass this section, and then later on we can go back into committee or upon the third reading we can have a discussion of the title.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
That was all I wished
to direct the minister's attention to.
Section 1 agreed to.
On section 2-Definitions.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: The minister spoke to me about this bill, but since then I have heard a little criticism that the proposed name of the new department, "Department of Pensions and National Health," might suggest that it was taking over the control of pensions and would interfere with the time-honoured custom of having the pensions branch independent. I do not think that is the minister's intention, but there is a little criticism and perhaps a little misinterpretation in that regard.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I think that when we deal with the Pension Act that misconception will disappear. The pension commission will remain as they are at present, independent, but it is true that this department, in the course of its administrative work, will pay the cheques after the adjudication has been made.

Section agreed to.
Sections 3 to 5 inclusive agreed to.
On section 6, subsection 1, paragraph (b)- Selection and employment of staff.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
In view of the discretion with respect to employment, should all the positions mentioned be excluded from the operation of the Civil Service Act? The old act excluded employees that might be required from time to time. Now excluded we have:
Part time professional officers, or part or full time employees whose compensation is determined by rates payable for similar work in the locality in which such persons are employed.
Is it desirable to take these matters entirely out of the hands of the Civil Service Commission?

Pensions and National Health

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
There are certain
employees in and about our hospitals-attendants, engineers, carpenters, dietitians-that would not be considered permanent but part time or full time employees. They would be paid the prevailing rate. Provision is made later in the bill to take care of those who become permanently attached.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I quite realize that, but
as subsection (b) reads, it provides:
for the selection and employment of such part time professional officers or part or full time employees whose compensation
may be paid. That certainly would look towards permanent positions. That is why I am directing attention to the amendment. I quite agree that if you hire a man for a day's work it is not a matter for the Civil Service Commission at all; but when it comes to full time employment, I see no reason why you should exclude the operations of the Civil Service Act.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: There are certain classes of employees that I do not think we wish to engage permanently. Take your attendants in the hospitals, their positions change very rapidly, as no doubt my hon. friend who has had experience knows. Then it is debatable whether your nursing staff should be made permanent; they change from time to time of their own will or from necessity. Those employed as carpenters, engineers or firemen would be considered part time employees, or what are known as prevailing rate employees. The same principle applies in other departments of government.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Quite so; but this substitutes for the section printed on the opposite side of the bill something different in principle:
and the creation for this purpose of appropriate positions,
That puts in the hands of the minister the power to create a full time position and disregard the Civil Service Commission; whereas the section that is being repealed provides:
that the employees selected and employed under the authority of the said regulations shall, as far as practicable, be classified by the minister in accordance with the schedules of classes of positions set forth in the civil service classification, and shall be paid such rates of salary as are thereby described, and the said regulations shall, as regards salary increases, leave of absence, promotions and resignations, conform as nearly as practicable to the regulations made under the Civil Service Act, 1918.
The effect of the amendment is disastrous to the minister-not my hon. friend, but the minister who happens to be in charge of the department-because under subsection (c) he will be creating the appropriate positions and
making appointments without regard to the Civil Service Act; whereas working side by side with the people so appointed will be those selected under the Civil Service Act at rates of pay provided by the Civil Service Commission. That, I think, is exactly what we are endeavouring to prevent. Before the minister asks us to adopt subsection (e) I suggest that he consider whether we are not making a retrograde step in replacing the relevant subsection in the old act by this subsection, which introduces patronage in its most vicious form with respect to a matter which should not be dealt with in that way.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
That is hardly
the situation. As a matter of fact the positions under the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment at the present time are outside the Civil Service Commission, and the appointments have been made by the governor-in-council on the advice of the minister. But we are preparing, through this legislation, to bring a portion at least of the service into permanency and under the Civil Service Commission. However, it has been felt that certain services are being rendered in the department with respect to which it would be very difficult to make permanent appointments; in fact it would not be good for the service. In the application of the present act the practices and usage of the Civil Service Commission have been followed by the department. Our classification is very much along the line of that of the Civil Service Commission, and the rates of pay are very much the same. This condition will continue under the new method. This is merely providing for a certain class which it would not seem wise to bring into the service permanently, and separate it from the class that eventually will be brought in permanently.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I desire to support what my hon. leader has just said. One of the subsections is as follows:
for the selection and employment of such part time professional officers, or part or full time employees,
If the words, " or full ", were not there I not think the section would be open to criticism. Let me read the passage with those words left out:
for the selection and employment of such part time professional officers or part time employees,
Worded that way there can be no doubt that it could not be suggested for a moment that any employee could be regarded as permanent; but the moment you introduce the words, "or full time", the employee could be appointed as permanent, although I
Pensions and National Health

am not assuming for a moment that the minister intends the section to bear this meaning. Therefore I would suggest that if he insert the word "temporary" before the word "employees" the situation might be met. May I read the subsection thus amended:
for the selection and employment of such part time professional officers, or part or full time temporary employees.
I think that would remove any thought that the minister, with the approval of the governor-in-council, is assuming the right to appoint permanent employees.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
If my hon. friend will
allow me to read the section as it was before, I think he will see that what is being done here is rather restrictive of the minister's power than an extension of it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
May I say to my hon. friend
that while we might interpret it now with the first draft before us, in the future nobody will be in that favourable position.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Not the first draft, but
the act we are amending.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
You do not have even that
before you after the consolidation of the statutes.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: My hon. friend misunderstands me. I am not using the previous act as a means of interpretation, but I am pointing out that the bill now before the house is more restrictive of the powers of the minister than is the previous act. My hon. friend quite properly pointed out that not only part time but full time employees are included in the present bill.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Who may be appointed by
the minister.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Under regulations. This
is a section regarding regulations. Pull time employees are limited to thosewhose compensation is determined by the rates payable for similar work in the locality in which such persons are employed.
Under the old act there was no provision at all, as to either part time or full time; the minister had power to pass regulations authorizing the selection and employment of officers, clerks and employees. There were therefore both part and full time employees under one regulation. Now they are separated into part time employees and full time employees. I take it that the reference to employees whose compensation is determined by the rates payable for similar work in the locality in which such persons are employed is to more or less casual labourers, transients, mechanics and so forth. This bill limits the minister as compared with the existing act.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: The minister suggests that this languagewhose compensation is determined by the rates payable for similar work in the locality in which such persons are employedwould indicate that they are not to be permanent. Is that the point?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: No.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Then I have missed the
point. I would say that when a full time employee is to be appointed this section merely indicates what he is to get; and having got it I suppose he continues to receive that compensation until perhaps he applies for an increase. If that is not the case then I have missed the point.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
The provision to which
my hon. friend refers, regarding part time and full time employees, is no wider than the act as it stands. The act which is being amended contains neither the adjective "part" nor the adjective "full" time; it uses simply the wrord "employees". This would permit the minister to employ persons either for an indefinite length of time or permanently. Full time employees under the present bill are only those whose compensation is determined by the rates payable for similar work in the locality in which such persons are employed.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Will the minister read
the latter part of the old section, the first portion of which he has quoted.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I am trying first to
answer my hon. friend (Mr. Boys). He suggests that the words "part time" and "full time" in some way or other extend the power of the minister. "Part time" and "full time", taken separately with this clause, limit rather than extend the power of the minister. But even if the language does not limit his power it goes no further than the present act.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: It does.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: If my hon. friend could convince a judge in that manner, I should be glad to have him as my advocate in the first civil case I had.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I am sure I could convince my hon. friend.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
The minister points out that
because of the existing act he does not think the bill we are about to pass has the effect and force we are contending for. Why therefore bother to discuss the present law? Let us take what the house is trying to pass and endeavour to construe it.

Pensions and National Health

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I thought that was what
my hon. friend was basing his argument upon. I thought he was arguing that the present bill extended the old act.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
That may be the effect, but
that is not my argument. I am endeavouring to ascertain the meaning of the legislation offered this committee, and in a word my point is this: the moment you insert the words " or full time employees", giving the minister power to appoint any full time employee, such an employee might remain indefinitely and would therefore become permanent.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: If he were satisfactory.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: But that is not what the minister intends, I am told. If that is so, why not put the matter beyond peradventure? If the minister can think of a better word I have no desire to press my suggestion. But if you say "or part or full time temporary employees" you exclude the thought of permanency, while at the same time the minister would have full power to appoint any employee, but only for temporary service.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: The minister might well make an explanation when he is dealing with two branches which will come under him and one of which up to the present time has been under the Civil Service Act. How is he going to distinguish between these two? He may take over a clerk from the Department of Health, who is under the Civil Service Act; and he may get another clerk from the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment, not under the act. In other words, the minister, in this bill is not making one change, except that he will have the appointment of every clerk and official who is under the Health Department. Notwithstanding the few words added in the section, he is going to have the appointment of every clerk and official in that department as well as in the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment. I cannot see where he has made any change.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: If my hon. friend will consult the bill he will find in the section with which we are dealing that the officers are under the department administering soldier affairs, while in part two he will find that the officers to be appointed in the health section are to be appointed under the Civil Service Act. I cannot see any objection to the word "temporary"-temporary employees-if it is considered necessary. Those I have in mind, and who were contemplated by the draughtsman, are part time .professional officers scattered throughout the country, probably medical men who give certain services to the returned men or pensioners, and who are receiving a partial or part time fee. I do not think anyone would suggest that these part time individuals should be considered permanent; they change from time to time. Then the full time employees-those whom my hon. friend designates full time "temporary" employees- are the class of men who work around the institutions, particularly in connection with hospitals, such as cooks, assistant cooks, ward attendants and so forth. It would not be wise to place them in the permanent class. It is not for me to say whether the term "full time temporary employees" is suitable or not. Personally I can see no great objection to it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: My hon. friend seems to agree with the idea I have expressed, and his only fear is that the word I have suggested may not be the best. If he can suggest anything wrong with it, I will not press it, although it seems to me to meet the situation.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: In the minister's interpretation of the words "full time," has he really the idea that these are permanent employees? Is the word "permanent" applicable to full time? Would it not be better to designate the class whom he wishes to have looked after under the term "full time"? The expressions "full time" and "permanency" are not by any means synonymous. There is a great difference between them.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I was just discussing this with the minister, and he tells me that the Department of Justice drew the bill and have gone over it with a great deal of care. As I have tried to point out to the committee, I am sure it does not extend the power of the minister beyond what it is now, and in fact with all due deference to my hon. friend I am sure that power is limited. That being so, it is not thought advisable to insert some word or some adjective without consulting the Department of Justice.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
If it were not for what has already happened I might be impressed by the suggestion that this draft has passed the scrutiny of certain officers of the Department of Justice, but not long ago a bill was introduced by the Minister of Trade and Commerce in which the same situation arose. That bill also had passed the scrutiny of departmental officials, but an amendment was suggested which may have been adopted; if it has not been accepted I think it will be, and it is possible that in the scrutiny of this
Pensions and National Health

bill this point has not been considered by the officers of the department. It does not make much difference to me; my purpose is simply this: I do not believe the minister should have the power which he receives under this section, and to be fair to him he does not pretend to seek such power. All I want to do is to have it put beyond question, and it s'eems to me that what I am suggesting would achieve that end. However, why not let this subsection stand and if there is any objection to the wrnrd I would be glad to hear it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Very well; I would suggest that we let subsection (b) stand and proceed with the bill.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: In the meantime would the minister make it more clear just what change is taking place in this act through these amendments with respect to the control by the minister or by the governor in council over the appointment of the personnel of this department? As I understand it, because of the alleged temporary nature of the department, under the old legislation every single member of the personnel was excluded from the operations of the Civil Service Act. I would like the minister to tell us what change he is making and whom he is bringing under the operations of the Civil Service Act now.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: We are of the opinion that the time has arrived when this department should be amalgamated with the Department of Health, and following that amalgamation and re-organization in the course of a little time we should be able definitely to define those positions which we consider as necessary to carry on the functions of the department, and which should be considered as permanent at least during the lifetime of this generation. This class of which we are speaking never will be considered permanent, but during the summer the executive officers, some of the clerical staff and others of the professional staff will be classified, and next May they will become permanent. During the interval there will be a selection of those who are to become permanent, because section 16 provides that in May, 1929, the Civil Service Act, which has been held in abeyance, will function.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Where does that appear?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: In section 16 on page 7. I would suggest that we pass from subsection (b) to the next subsection.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: And subsection (b) will stand?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
In defining the
outside service, does the minister mean that all the present outside service, or at least those connected with the hospitals, will be what are called full time temporary employees? The minister mentioned carpenters and plumbers who might be working around the hospital, and also referred to dieticians. I imagine that a dietician would be considered permanent, whereas a carpenter or plumber would be needed only from time to time. There is no such thing in a hospital as a full time carpenter, but a dietician is an important member of a hospital staff.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: A dietician would be a full time professional officer.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I wish to
make it quite clear to the minister that in allowing this subsection to stand at this stage, before the debate has been concluded, he may be making a mistake. I do not object to the subsection standing, but there is a good deal more information which we might secure and there may be a good deal of criticism to be offered, which might help the minister in making what alterations he may have in mind. We do not want to be prejudiced in any way; we would not want anyone to say that we allowed this subsection to stand without criticism.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
We will allow it to stand until we are in committee again.
Paragraph (b) stands.
Paragraph (c), (d) and (e) agreed to.
Paragraph (f): Reciprocal and other arrangements with other governments.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I think this subsection was before the special committee, and it was inserted in the bill subject to any recommendations or amendments which might be proposed by that committee.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I believe that is right.
Subsection (f) agreed to.
On section 6. subsection 1, paragraph (g)- Sheltered emploj^ment of ex-members of forces, etc.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Just a moment,
Mr. Chairman. Under this act, are you going to take the responsibility for the burying of those in destitute circumstances?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Of course there is the
Last Post fund.

Pensions and National Health

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
They are most
interested in the non-pensioned soldier who may die. * The pensioner will have burial under the provisions which exist. The Last Post fund is an outside organization which is supported by a grant from the government from time to time.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
It might come under
this, if you do not mention the pensioner.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: It might.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would
like to ask the minister in respect to clause (g), will that not apply to persons who are in destitute circumstances and yet require medical attention?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I do not think
the section definitely provides for employment for ex-service men who are not pensioners.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: No, medical attention.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
No, it does not.
They are supposed to be pensioners. The only treatment provided there was:
The treatment of former members of the forces classified as wholly incurable or chronically recurrent cases needing institutional care; for the provision of measures of unemployment relief to ex-members of the forces and their dependents, and for the payment of compensation in respect of industrial accidents; the whole subject to such appropriations as parliament may provide.
Treatment to-day in our institutions is confined really to those who are pensioners. It is true that by regulations the governor in council can extend and give treatment to those who are indigent and require such treatment. We did that in regard to a certain class last summer, and those orders were placed upon the table. We found throughout Canada a number of cases of exservice men who had contracted certain diseases overseas, who were totally disabled and in poor circumstances, and provision was made for that class last year. But generally speaking a man to be entitled to treatment in our hospitals must have been considered by the pension board eligible for pension, and therefore eligible for treatment.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would like
to bring to the attention of the minister the fact that we have many cases in Canada in which returned men require hospital treatment; where it cannot be claimed that their trouble is attributable to war service. I would like to see the minister at this session of parliament make some provision for that class. I quite understand that you must be very
careful in dealing with such cases, but I know many to which such consideration should be given irrespective of the fact that their condition is not attributable to war service. In my opinion this country should give them medical treatment.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I believe extensive recommendations have been given to the committee which is dealing with soldier affairs. I think the soldier body has gone into that very thoroughly. At any rate, the governor in council has power to make provision for medical treatment.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I would like to draw the attention of the minister to quite a large number of cases of returned soldiers who allowed a period of years to pass by, after they returned from the front, without bothering any of the pension boards. Now we find that often for five or six years there is no medical history whatsoever for these unfortunate people; and the result is that when their cases are brought up for consideration they can get no relief. I think that in this bill we should consider carefully those men who, after their return, had courage and grit enough, not to worry the pension board but to go right into work. After five or six years they are broken down, and their cases are really often worse than those presented to the pension board. When these cases come before the board, as many will, I would like the minister, to see that they receive such consideration as will result in relief being given. On that point I would like to draw the attention of the minister to this. It is a pity that a great number of the returned soldiers, ignorant of the methods of obtaining relief, have to come to the ordinary member of parliament, who is placed under great difficulties in obtaining the knowledge necessary to present to the board of pension commissioners the cases of these men; and I think, sir, in the department that has to do with returned soldiers there should be some particular person set apart, whose duty it should be to go to the aid of these men, and thus save them trouble, anxiety and loss.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
In reply to my
hon. friend, it is true that many of the returned men are experiencing difficulties on account of their medical file or sheet not showing that they had had treatment over a period of years. It requires very considerable investigation to secure that evidence but it is necessary that some evidence be obtained. I know from the work of the pension board that inquiries of that character are going on from day to day, and in order to assist the soldier in his inquiries and in preparing his case,

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
How many advisers are
there in British Columbia?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
There is one in
Vancouver city covering the mainland of the province of British Columbia and one in Victoria covering Vancouver island. There is one in Ai'berta, one in Saskatchewan, one in Manitoba, two or three in Ontario, two in Quebec, one in New Brunswick, one in Nova Scotia, and one in Prince Edward Island.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: As this is such an important matter and northern and central British Columbia comprise such an immense area, would it not be advisable to have an adviser for that portion of the province situated at some central point such as Prince Rupert or Smithers? The soldiers have so much land in the north country that they would have to come hundreds of miles to a central point and these unfortunate people do not know how to get in touch with the advisers.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Where the work
is accumulating and not being dealt with rapidly, we may increase the number or appoint men temporarily to relieve the situation. There is something in what the hon. member says with regard to the western provinces. The distances are great; the men are spread throughout the community, and it takes time to deal with the different cases. Although we have an excellent man in Manitoba, he has found his work has got behind arid it has been necessary for the department to give assistance to bring his work up to date.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Somehow the system is not
very effective after all, and I think it is three years ago now since I brought this matter to the attention of the minister. I know of cases that, we are all satisfied, are due

to war experience, where men have not yet been able to get on the pension list. In my constituency there was one one man who was suffering when he returned, but although I brought his case repeatedly before the minister and the pension board and although he is totally disabled, he is unable to get any relief from the board. The last I knew of him was that he was in a hospital in Winnipeg. Who is paying the hospital authorities I do not know. That is only one case and there are others.	I have always
taken the ground in this house that as regards anyone who has seen active service at the front and who has been disabled, this country is under obligation to provide and care for him when he is in want. I think the act should be made a little more elastic so as to cover these cases and so that the benefit of the doubt will all be given to the returned soldier. These men are suffering daily, feeling that they are humiliated by receiving charity.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
The matters
referred to by my hon. friend would more properly come under the Pension Act which is now being reviewed by a special committee of the house. That committee has heard evidence and expressions of opinion similar to that expressed by my hon. friend, and no doubt it will give careful consideration to such representations.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
If I recall aright,
there was brought to our attention in one of the committees this morning the case of a man who is not able to establish clearly that his impairment of health was directly due to war service. He is being assisted during the winter months for a short time, but after that he is thrown on public charity and the city of Winnipeg has to maintain him. In cases of that kind I think the least we can do for a man who has served at the front is to see he is taken care of. In this particular instance he is perhaps a little below the average mental standard so that there is all the more need for some care to be exercised during the whole of the year. Again I would plead that the regulations should be broadened out to take care of this class of case.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I believe the question was already asked by an hon. member on this side in regard to provision being made for the burial of a deceased returned man, but I did not catch the answer. Is there any such provision in this bill or any other to take care of the burial expenses of a returned man who is in destitute circumstances?

Pensions and National Health

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Paragraph (g) of clause 6 in the thirty-seventh line reads:
For providing burial expenses for ex-members of the forces who die in destitute circumstances.
That covers the case.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I understood the minister to say that that referred to those who are pensioned. Does that cover every case of destitution, because if it does it leaves the minister and the department open to many requests and there is no use for the last post fund?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: The clause is one providing for regulations which may cover these cases.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Is this the first provision that has been made for such cases or has there been heretofore any such provision?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: It is the same section.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I know of a case that happened within a few miles of my town of a returned man who had taken up land under the soldier settlement board and who had a good prospective crop on the quarter-section but who before the crop was harvested, took ill and died. He had no money in hand or in sight except what would be realized from the crop and the people of the community had to go around and raise funds to cover his burial expenses. I was asked some time ago to ascertain whether there was provision in the act to take care of such cases.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: This clause will empower the government to make provision for every ex-service man in destitute circumstances. The policy of the government to date has been to bury those who die of pensionable disabilities providing it is necessary to do so. In addition to that we have been supporting what is known as the Last Post fund. That is an organization throughout Canada which has been doing excellent work by providing funds for burial expenses in the locality where the death may occur. We have been supporting that organization by a grant to the executive and in addition last year by supplementing their expenditures where they failed to secure sufficient funds for the work which they were doing.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: May I also remind the hon. member that he has the word of . the Prime Minister that he would like to know of any such case that was unprovided for under the Last Post fund?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: That is true.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: In the event of the death of an ex-service man in destitute circumstances, to whom is application made for burial expenses?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Ordinarily it would be through the local branch of the Last Post fund in the various provinces.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Would that necessarily be to the headquarters at Vancouver?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: It would come from the local branch to the provincial headquarters, and from there to the central organization. There would be no difficulty; it is working very well.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Does the soldiers' adviser make periodical trips throughout the province or must all communications be addressed to him at Vancouver?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Usually I think the communications have been sent in to his residence, but if it is found that there is a large number of claims outstanding in any one district, and a request is' made that the adviser should go in there, and the department think it advisable even though it is a considerable distance from his home, if the service to be rendered justifies it, he would be sent in there and his expenses paid. But I do not think the soldiers' adviser has been travelling very far from his centre.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I am sure he has not.
British Columbia is a pretty vast territory, and does not the minister think it advisable to suggest that the soldiers' adviser make periodical trips to the various branches of the legion, where he could receive complaints and applications? I say that because I have no less than one dozen different matters which have been brought to my attention from returned men, and I have been in correspondence with the service bureau here, and I must say that I have had excellent service, but it does occur to me that if the soldiers' adviser would go into the interior of the province of British Columbia, he could get into closer touch with the men and ascertain from the applicants just what the basis of their claims was.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
If it is found that there is a large number of applications from, say, the Kootenay district, Rossland, Nelson, Trail, and so on, there would be no difficulty in arranging to have the soldiers' adviser make the trip in there. The whole service is guided by the number of applications that have to be considered by the pension board or by the appeal board, and if it was shown that there was a large number of applicants
Pensions and National Health

in the Kootenay district, for instance, who could conveniently be seen by the adviser going in there, I do not see any objection to that; in fact, I would be quite anxious that he should do so.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: The members from British Columbia must have received numerous communications from returned men throughout the province, from scattered districts, and it would seem to me very desirable that the adviser should visit the different districts. There are many of the men who do not know that there is such an adviser.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
What is the minister's interpretation of the following paragraph in paragraph (g) of section 6:
