for the treatment of former members of the forces classified as wholly incurable or chronically recurrent cases needing institutional care.
How broad is that?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I noticed that myself.
The first part of the paragraph provides generally for the treatment of everybody, and these words seem to refer particularly to those who need institutional care, those whose disease is wholly incurable or chronically recurrent. But if my hon. friend will look at section 5, he will see that it gives the minister power in reference to any matters assigned to him relating in any way to the care, treatment or reestablishment in civil life of all persons-my hon. friend will note that it says, "of all"-who since the first day of August, 1914, served in the naval, military or air forces. Then section 6 (a) provides for the control and management of any hospital, workshop, home, school, or other institution, owned, acquired, or used by His Majesty for the training, care or treatment of any person at all, not simply those mentioned in paragraph (g).

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Section 6 simply
states that, subject to the approval of the governor in council, the minister may make such regulations as he may deem necessary and advisable. Then paragraph (g) provides:
For providing burial expenses for ex-mejnbers of the force who die in destitute circumstances.
But there is no provision in the act to take care of such cases as I mentioned. The minister may make provision for taking care of them, but I would like to have something definite from the minister whether he thinks provision should be made for such cases, and to what extent such provision should be made.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I have stated the practice that is being followed at the present time in regard to these cases. There have

been representations made recently to the committee that is now sitting on soldier questions, but whether they will make further recommendations or not, I am not sure. With regard to the case my hon. friend speaks of, I expect that the soldier settler was not a pensioner, because I think that the men selected to go on the land were selected on account of their physical fitness and because it was thought they would best succeed as farmers. So I do not think that he would be a pensioner, and under those circumstances the case would probably be met by the Last Post fund, to which the government subscribes and which it supplements.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
No. In the case I
mentioned the man was not a pensioner, I believe. He had purchased land from the soldier settlement board and had a good prospective crop, but it was still standing, and the soldier settlement board commandeered all the crop, and all the machinery, and all the movable assets that this settler had. There was nothing whatsoever left to pay his funeral expenses, and the undertaker would not undertake the funeral expenses until they were guaranteed to him, and the expenses had to be raised by public subscription in that community. It appears to me that that is a disgraceful situation, and if our statutes are so framed that an ex-service man cannot have a decent burial, there is certainly something wrong with the statutes. I would like to emphasize to the minister the need of having something definite and specific to take care of such cases.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
May I inquire of the
minister whether the services of the soldiers' adviser at Vancouver, for instance, would be available to soldiers who bring appeals from the revaluation of their land. That is a question which is causing a good deal of uneasiness in British Columbia. I understand that there will be quite a large number of these appeals, because the soldier settlers are not satisfied as a general thing with the decisions which have been given lately. Now, for the ordinary man to appeal to the exchequer court presents many difficulties, and a great many of these men are not in a position to pay for legal expenses. Neither are they capable of paying their expenses to Ottawa to appear before the exchequer court. If hearings could be held in an informal manner near their places of residence, returned men might conduct their cases in person. It seems to me advisable that they should have the privilege of using the soldiers' adviser to help

Pensions and National Health
them on the appeal. I think this adviser would do his best for them, although he is retained by the department.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
If my hon. friend will
permit me, the soldiers' advisers, as my colleague has said, are appointed on the recommendation of the soldiers' organizations; they are really the servants of the soldiers.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I am glad to hear
that. The minister probably knows how many appeals there will be, although this matter does not come in his department. I have had correspondence with the Minister of Immigration (Mr. Forke) on the subject. He has been kind enough to answer certain questions which I put to him from the secretary of one of the returned men's organizations in Langley municipality. But the fact remains that at present there does not seem to be any provision at all to take care of these returned men whe appeal from decisions in reference to the valuation of their land. At the risk of repeating myself, I suggest that the minister and his colleagues should take into consideration the advisability of allowing these men to have the advantage of the services of the soldiers' adviser.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Will not the minister consider having the soldiers' adviser make these trips? May I ask the name of the gentleman?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I shall be glad
to make inquiries and consider the advisability of the soldiers' adviser making trips into the interior. The name of the adviser on the mainland is Captain Ian Mackenzie. My hon. friend speaks of the utilization of the soldiers' adviser to assist the soldier settler in his claim. That is a new phase. Heretofore the soldiers' advisers have been appointed to advise and assist ex-members of the force in matters pertaining to their re-establishment, care and treatment and pensions. His suggestion may be worthy of consideration.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: That would come within his jurisdiction, it seems to me.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: It may be.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I think it is unfortunate that this discussion should be taking place while the special committee is sitting. As to care and treatment, I do not think the minister can assure the member for Acadia (Mr. Gardiner) that that includes everybody, notwithstanding what the Minister of National Defence has said, because the clause he took up deals with the matters which shall be referred to him, and he knows that up to the 56103-156
present time the care and treatment of those not pensionable does not come under him. It seems to me that the settlers' case which has been mentioned should not be allowed to drop. When the time comes the hon. member should take it up with the minister in charge of the soldier settlement board and insist that they look after the burial in such cases. They took every cent that he had saved during the war and invested it in his farm; in fact, they cleaned him out. The hon. member should insist that from this day forward the soldier settlement board see to it that no ex-service man doing settlement duty, in the unfortunate event of death, be neglected and his burial left to the charity of other people.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I did intend to ask the member for Kindersley (Mr. Carmichael) for a little more information in regard to the case he brought to our notice. On the facts as presented by him it is a deplorable case. Did the man die on his farm, or had everything been sold before his death?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: The settler to whom I referred enlisted with the first contingent, served throughout the war, and came back unwounded and unpensionable. He bought a quarter-section of land under the soldier settlement board, put nearly the whole of it under cultivation, and had a good prospective crop; but he took sick and died, I think in July or August, before the crop was harvested. I believe he did owe some dues to the settlement board because of the bad times. They took possession of his stock, crop, machinery and everything he had, as well as the land. The poor fellow left no money behind and was buried by some charitable persons.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
All I can say, Mr. Chairman, is that this should not have happened. And it would not have happened had I received any information in regard to the matter. My instructions to all the staff of the soldier settlement board, from the superintendent down to the supervisors, are that the soldier shall have the best treatment we can give him, that whenever doubt exists he is to be given the benefit of the doubt, and that if there is any possibility of his being able to make good ten years from now he shall not lose his farm. I think that satisfied soldier settlers five or ten years from now are of much greater value to the country than any monetary collection that can be made at the present time. I will make inquiries into this particular case and find out just what has happened. Somebody will get into trouble over it.



Pensions and National Health

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
In fairness to the
minister, I must state that this case happened before he took charge of the department. I am not charging him with any dereliction of duty whatever.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
But it might happen, and I know nothing of it.
Subsection (1) of section 6 agreed to.
On subsection (2)-Regulations to be laid before parliament.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I am not familiar with the facts of the case presented by the hon. member for Kindersley, but I do not think he is contending that had the officials of the soldier settlement board been appealed to they would have refused to advance the funeral expenses. I think his contention is that under the bill we are discussing somebody should be in a position to put up the necessary money at such a time.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: In paragraph (g), subsection 1 of section 6, there is a very important provision, that the minister may make regulations for the provision of measures of unemployment relief to ex-members of the forces and their dependants. Considering the many cases that are arising, and that exist at the present time, of unemployment among returned soldiers, I should like to know exactly what will be the measures of unemployment relief. Will these men be given jobs through the provincial governments, or will the relief be given in terms of financial aid, and for what period? This is a rather broad provision; it is a far-reaching statement covering a great extent of unemployment; because many returned soldiers to-day are badly in need of relief. One case came to my notice the other day of a returned man who has been incapaciated and is unfit to work. He has six children and his wife is supporting them and him as well. He cannot get employment; his case is chronic. I desire to know what may be expected when cases of this character are presented for relief.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
In the larger
centres where the provincial government maintains labour bureaus with a view to assisting the labourer in securing employment, the Dominion Labour department have what is known as the handicap section where the returned soldier who is handicapped by disability or disease may make application. It is the duty of these officers to try to locate the individual in some industry in that vicinity. That work is going on throughout Canada. In addition to that we have what is known as sheltered unemployment in our

vetcraft shops. This is limited employment. At the present time between 245 and 250 men, considered ordinarily as unemployable in the labour market, are provided for in this *way. We have had also in Montreal, Toronto and Vancouver committees who have been carrying on similar work, endeavouring through their individual efforts or jointly to induce employers of labour to provide employment for those who are disabled among the returned soldiers. Again, the government is assisting industrialists to employ the partly disabled soldier, and has for some time now been providing for the payment of compensation in connection with industrial accidents. That is to say, we arrange with the various compensation boards to provide for the insurance and payment necessary to carry these men under the boards, relieving the manufacturer in this respect. The government has carried on this activity in all the provinces, the expenditure last year having been i>75,000. This has made it possible for many men to secure employment in the various industries, inasmuch as we have been absorbing that cost.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: The Minister of National Defence drew my attention to section 5. I would ask him whether he thinks that in this particular section there will be sufficient power to take care of the cases I have already mentioned. I am keenly interested in the matter, and I desire some definite information as to whether these people will secure adequate treatment.

I want to call the attention of the minister to a point in this section which is a bit obscure to me. He may be able to enlighten me, but at the moment it does not appear to me to be correct. I refer to that portion of the section included in lines 25, 26 and 27, which provides for the carrying of the members of the staff of the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment into the new orientation of the two departments. The closing two lines of the first paragraph are:
-and shall thereafter become subject in all respects to the Civil Service Act.
But in the clause preceding those two lines are words to this effect:
-be thereby appointed to the Department of Pensions and National Health at the salaries and in the classification fixed under the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment Act,
In other words, while you are carrying this staff forward into the new department and placing them under the Civil Service Act, you are fixing their classification and salaries as under the old act, thus putting them more or less into conflict with the Civil Service Act and the Civil Service Commission system. Would it not be fairer, and in order to avoid complaints in the future would it not be more desirable to say that you carry them into the new department and place them under the Civil Service Act both as regards salary and classification? It might be thought advisable in some individual case, but in the main it is an unwise principle to introduce into the civil service a department the salaries and classifications of which are different from those in other departments. That is really what you are doing; you are perpetuating a difference. Wherever you interfere with the general system of the civil service you introduce more or less confusion and make it more difficult for the Civil Service Commission to discharge

My idea is, as far as possible, to bring them into conformity and uniformity as far as the Civil Service Act is concerned.

I should like to emphasize that we have the right to determine the conditions upon which divorce should be granted, and further, if those conditions are made rigid enough, I am inclined to think that we may not have quite so many divorce bills before us in the future. speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make it clear that I am dealing with this bill as a sort of test case. There is a very large number of these bills on the order paper; I had no opportunity of reading the evidence relating to these scores of bills, and as I glanced through the bills I took this one as the first that occurred to me as seeming to answer the purpose I had in view. I have no idea that the people involved here are in any worse case than a large number of the others who may be affected by similar bills

on the order paper, and I have not intended in bringing forward this motion to give them preferential treatment. This is the motion of which I have given notice:
That the said bill be not now read a third time, but that it be referred back to the committee of the whole for the purpose of amending it as follows:

(1)	That section one of the bill be amended by adding the following words thereto:
"and the said Winnifred Osborne Sinclair shall have the custody of their child and the said William Henry Gimblett shall pay annually to Winnifred Osborne Sinclair, for her support and maintenance, the sum of five hundred dollars, so long as she remains unmarried; and the sum of two hundred dollars annually for the support and education of their child."
(2)	That section two of the bill be amended by adding the following words thereto:
"Provided that this right shall be exercised only upon condition that she shall be previously examined by competent medical authority and pronounced free of venereal disease, and that William Henry Gimblett may marry again only upon the same condition."
Mr. Speaker, I notice that in the petition presented the following complaints were made:
That after her said marriage your petitioner lived and cohabited with the said William Henry Gimblett at the said city of Ottawa, in the province of Ontario, and that there is now living issue of the said marriage one child, viz:	William Henry Victor Gimblett, born
on the 16th day of November, 1924.
That in the year 1926, the said William Henry Gimblett committed adultery with various women whose names are unknown to your petitioner, but. as the result of such illicit intercourse, the said William Henry Gimblett contracted a loathsome sexual disease which he communicated to your petitioner, from which your petitioner is now suffering, and for which your petitioner is now receiving medical treatment.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that if this house is to continue the practice of granting divorce we ought to take all the circumstances into consideration. This woman has a child by the man from whom she seeks to obtain a divorce. That child, now something over four years of age, ought to remain in her custody. There is nothing in the bill which definitely determines the custody of the child. Further than that, if the woman has been so wronged the least we can do is to see that she be given something to maintain her during the years that she may remain unmarried. I have arbitrarily placed this at $500 a year. It is quite obvious that with no evidence before us as to the circumstances of either of them it is impossible to determine with any accuracy how much is needed; so I set a perfectly arbitrary figure. In the same way I have placed the maintenance of the child at $200, again an arbitrary figure but not an unreasonable one. In a proper divorce court there

Criminal Code Amendment
would be provision as to the manner in which these sums should be paid, and further than that, there would be penalties for their nonpayment. It seems to me that the best course at this time would be to put the motion in the form I have suggested, without going into details, because we are here simply determining upon a principle. I will appeal to the members of this house that if a man has in this way wronged a woman, if he has left this child unprovided for, if he has actually passed disease on to his wife, the least we can do is to require that he shall pay a sum sufficient to maintain his wife and his child. That seems to be a reasonable thing. As it is now we give to her the right to marry again, and inferentially we give him the right to marry again, but we make no provision for her maintenance, and I think it' is only a fair thing that we should do so.
Moreover, according to the evidence presented, the man was diseased and the woman is now suffering from the disease communicated to her. Are we going to tell her that she has a right to marry again in the diseased condition, and worse, that the man has the opportunity of marrying again?
I was very glad to have my attention directed to the fact that there is now being considered by the senate a bill, letter D, to make venereal disease an impediment to marriage. I want to congratulate the hon. senators for considering such a bill as that. Whether we do that in a general way or not, it seems to me that the least we can do is to insist upon it in this case, where we already have the situation clearly before us in the evidence. I make this motion in the interest of the public and in the interest of the parties concerned.	.
It is nine o'clock.

On section 1-Unlawful associations. Publishing seditious books, etc.

I do not propose again
to go over the ground that has been so often gone over before, but it does not follow that because legislation is not used it is therefore bad. There are in the criminal code not many but some sections that have never been
used, with respect to which offences have not . arisen. This section was inserted in order to meet an extraordinary situation which we hope will not again obtain in this country, but it might obtain; it might prevail, and when it does, the section should be in the code to be used.
I will make only one suggestion to the minister, namely, that the section might well be revised, if there is any doubt about the matter, to make it clear that it has no application to labour unions. In days of unrest, disquietude and uncertainty to have in the criminal code a section to which recourse may be had in the event of the occasion arising, can never be a bad thing.
I believe the statute was originally drawn by one who is not now a member of this house, and that he said that to make it abundantly clear that labour unions were not included would not be a very difficult task. I do not like the idea of repealing this statute in its entirety, an idea which is attributable not to any fear of the statute but rather to the undertaking which was given some two years ago that the statute would be repealed and which was embodied in a letter given by the Prime Minister to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) and read in the house so that it might be recorded in Hansard. But for that, I fancy the necessity for repeal of the measure would not be so apparent nor the reasons so urgent to bring about the end which is now sought.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I move to amend Bill
No. 191 by adding thereto the following sections:
2.	The said act is amended by inserting after section 133 thereof the following:
133 A.
No one shall be deemed to have a seditious intention only because he intends in good faith,

(a)	to show that His Majesty has been misled or mistaken in his measures; or
(b)	to point out errors or defects in the government or constitution of the United Kingdom or of any part of it or of Canada or of any province thereof or in either house of parliament of the United Kingdom or of Canada or in any legislature or in the administration of justice; or to excite His Majesty's subjects to attempt to procure by lawful means the alteration of any matter in the state; or
(c)	to point out, in order to their removal, matters which are producing or have a tendency to produce feelings of hatred and ill will between different classes of His Majesty's subjects.

Criminal Code Amendment
Perhaps the minister will explain just what this means.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The purpose of the
amendment is to restore that part of the criminal code relating to sedition as it was prior to 1919. Those provisions have also been voted by the house five times.
This section?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

Is this amendment the
act as it was in 1919?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes-"two years".

There is only one observation I have to make and that is with respect to paragraph (b):
No one shall be deemed to have a seditious intention only because he intends in good faith to point out errors or defects. . . in the administration of justice.
That is a very broad way in which to express the matter, and certainly some of the prosecutions that have taken place in Great Britain could not be maintained in the light of that section. To prove bad faith is almost always impossible. Perhaps the minister knows from experience the crown officers have always said that the question of proving good or bad faith is one of those matters that are so difficult, it is almost hopeless to expect to succeed. Bad faith is a state of mind, and to prove a state of mind can usually be done only by expressions. If a man then says: The expressions I used were only for the purpose of directing attention to something in order that it might be remedied, in most instances you would say that is good faith; whereas he may have in fact the worst of bad faith in connection with the matter. I cannot but think the observations I made a few moments ago apply with even greater force to this. If in the light of knowledge and experience it is thought desirable to strengthen the hands of the law, not necessarily by bringing men within the purview of it but by declaring that under certain circumstances an offence is being committed, that provision may never be called into use; but while it is there the effect is salutary and you have in your hands a weapon that will enable the officers of the law to maintain peace, order and good government in the country when they are being threatened. That is why the legislation was enacted, and that is why it should remain on the statute book. If there be in the measure any ambiguity by which labour unions may be thought to be affected, that should be removed, but we should not reenact the old law simply because of promises that have been made.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not agree that the change was made in the light of knowledge and experience. As I said the other day, the change was made in a moment of panic. The three readings of the bill took place one afternoon inside of half an hour. I admit of course there was unrest at the time; but we cannot say that this was a very well-considered piece of legislation, and the fact that the statute has never served any purpose, because no proceeding has ever been instituted under it, shows it is not necessary to have it on the statute book. As regards the wording of the amendment, it is exactly what it was in the criminal code of Canada prior to 1919. After all I do not think we should be much in favour of limitation of free speech, provided that it is done in a constitutional way and merely as a matter of criticism against the government.
I agree as to that.
I should like to remind the Minister of Justice that he himself was a consenting party to the passing of this act, and the members behind him were also consenting parties.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not remember.
Yes, he was. I was in the house at the time.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I cannot say no, but
perhaps I have since seen the error of my ways.

It is remarkable that the same light that came over Saul of Tarsus should come over the Minister of Justice and his followers, especially at a time when political exigencies demanded that he secure support from certain quarters. I should like to ask the minister to-day, disregarding the political necessity that called forth this promise from the government, what demand there is behind this legislation.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
My friend was not here
the other night when we discussed this matter. As I said at the time, all the labour unions in Canada and all the men who have had anything to do with the labour movement in this country have been asking since 1919 for the repeal of this legislation. They have come in delegations-
No.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Do not say no. I have
been a minister since 1921, and I know that along with other members of the government I have received every year delegations representative of labour, asking for the repeal of this legislation. They think that it is a

Criminal Code Amendment
danger to the working of the labour unions. They set forth, and I think they are right in doing so, that the common law concerning sedition is quite sufficient to provide for any prosecution of seditious libel, seditious utterance, or seditious conspiracy.

The minister has admitted that it has created no hardship, and surely he should be the last man to remove anything from the statute book which, while working no hardship, creates respect for law and order. If it has done no harm it may do some good in preserving respect for law and order in this country, which is something every law-abiding citizen desires to see. I cannot see how the minister can have had such a change of heart since he and his whole party were a party to putting this on the statute books in 1919. But ever since they have been trying to kick it out and get rid of it, just, because my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre demands that that be done.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Not at all.

That was the genesis
of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I think a similar bill
was introduced before my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre was a member of this house.

Yes, it was following a
letter from him that the government promised to repeal this legislation.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
No. Similar legislation
was introduced before he was a member of this house, I believe.
The government did not agree to repeal it before he demanded it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Oh yes, we did.

Now that the minister has
admitted seeing the light-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not admit having
seen the light because I do not agree that I have supported the legislation. I was not a member of the government that passed it.

I am sorry that the Conservative party has not yet seen the light on this matter. The question has been asked, who is asking for the repeal of this particular legislation? I would like to know who ever asked for this legislation in 1919.
Parliament, unanimously.

Who came to parliament
and asked for it in 1919?
The Prime Minister.

I do not know who was
Prime Minister then. I do not know whether Sir Robert Borden was in the house at that time.

Then the Acting Prime
Minister.

The Acting Prime Minister
may have asked for it, but there was no organization that came to parliament and asked for it. It was put on the statute book possibly at the mere whim of the then Prime Minister or Acting Prime Minister. But in this case, behind parliament there is the whole labour movement asking for the repeal of this legislation, and a great many people outside.

The section has been
passed, and my hon. friend is only obstructing the passing of the bill.

I am not obstructing it.
The obstruction comes from hon. gentlemen to my right on this side of the house, and from another house very closely associated with the minority in this house.

That is a statement the
hon. gentleman has no right to make. The rules of this house are clear on that.

If the rules of the house
debar me from making that statement, I am sorry that I made it, but I would make it outside.
Certainly, and that is why sections like this are in the code.

The labour unions have asked for the repeal of this legislation. I believe it has been stated in this house that the British law has not been used since it was put on the statute books, and I think it has been argued that it should be there in case of emergency. Now if there was an emergency in this country in 1919, and the old law was able to convict, why was this law necessary at all? That is something I should like to hear from members of the legal profession. I should like them to tell us a little more about that, but they deal only in generalities.
This law dealing with sedition does not at all create any respect for law and order; it has just the very opposite effect. I could go into the library of any hon. gentleman who has spoken on this question and I could find there seditious literature within the meaning of this act. I could take the Bible in their homes and find passages in it which would be construed as being absolutely sedititous under this section of the criminal code.

That is nonsense.
Criminal Code Amendment

If it was desired I could
point to passages in the Bible that would be considered absolutely seditious under this section of the criminal code. That being the. case, how can any person in this house argue that a law of this kind creates respect for law? It has the very opposite effect. If you want to create respect for law, the laws must be just in their character. I claim that this is a most unjust law, and that it operates unfairly and harshly on a section of the people of this country. I think the best thing you can do to create respect for law in this country is to repeal this law, which passed this house, I understand, in the space of twenty minutes. I would ask any hon. member of this house who wants the people of Canada to have respect for law in this country, how he can expect them to have respect for the law when a bill is given three readings and becomes the law of this land in the space of twenty minutes? We are supposed to be a deliberative assembly, and to give time and consideration to important questions.
That shows there was no opposition to it.

It shows a good deal more
than that. It shows that it was railroaded through this house.

It could not be if there
was opposition to it.

I am inclined to think from
the knowledge that has come to me from sources which I believe to be fairly reliable, that my latter contention may be the more correct of the two. I understand that at the time this law was passed, assurances were given to certain members of this house, that there was nothing of an important character in it. On account of those promises, the then leader of the opposition, a gentleman who is not now a member of this house-
To whom is my hon. friend referring?
Mr. D. D. McKenzie.
My hon. friend mentions the dead, of course.

I believe the fact is on record -and during the election of 1921 the same statement was made by that gentleman in Nova Scotia-that he let the bill go through on certain assurances given, to him by the then leader of this house. I mention that only to show the methods that were used to pass this legislation. If hon. gentlemen de-

sire to see respect for law in this country, they should see to it that laws are put on the statute book that the people of this country can respect.

As a matter of fact, my hon. friend's somewhat for him, moderate tirade is wholly unjustifiable. We have already passed this section, and I submit that he and others were out of order in discussing it. But if there is to be allowed a discussion in which the motives of those who were present when this law was passed, are to be called in question, we have at least the right to say a word or two in justification of our action.
The amendment was not railroaded through the house at all. I was in the house at the time, and I recall the circumstances perfectly well. There was unanimity of opinion in this house that it was absolutely necessary that there should be some amendment to the criminal code to make it possible to deal with a situation that had never occurred in Canada before, a situation which had up to that time seemed impossible to occur in a country such as this, but which did arise entirely out of the new revolutionary methods obtaining in certain parts of Europe and Asia.
The question whether or not this legislation was carefully considered is not open to dispute. The legislation was most carefully drafted, after very thorough consideration by the law officers of the crown, and in the face of conditions which made perfectly clear the nature of the legislation that was required to deal with the situation. It was not a question of theory, of carrying out anybody's ideals, whims or wishes; it was legislation carefully drafted and prepared after careful consideration by those competent to do so. It was then brought to the house, fully explained, and accepted by the house without a single word of opposition as far as I recollect, and I am certain I am correct in saying this.
It does not follow that this or that member must be saddled with the full responsibility of that measure. I am not aware of anyone repudiating responsibility for it. The point is that it was accepted by the house. Now it is wholly unfair and inaccurate to say that the bill was railroaded through the house on the strength of certain assurances, as my hon. friend says. I Submit that he has nothing whatsoever to back up his Statement that assurances were given either to the late D. D. McKenzie, who was then temporary leader of the opposition, or to any other member of the house. I was then and have been since in close contact with the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen, who was at that time

Criminal Code Amendment
more or less active in the drafting of the legislation, and I have never on any occasion heard him mention directly or indirectly that any such undertaking was given, and I am pretty certain he would have told some of us if that had been the case. That statement has never been made before when the matter was being discussed and particularly when the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen was in the house and well able to look after himself.
The statement I referred to was made by the late Mr. McKenzie himself.

Mr. McKenzie has been out of the house for nearly eight years. He ' is now dead, and we have no chance of discussing the matter with him. I sat with Mr. McKenzie while he was a member from 1911 to 1921, and I knew him well enough to be certain that he would not object to that legislation were he here to-night. In my estimation it is' not in violation of Mr. McKenzie's attitude towards such questions.
He certainly objected to it in 1921 when the elections took place in Nova Scotia.

My hon. friend would do much better if he would bring the record. However, I am not going to enter into a discussion on that point; it is1 not relevant, and has no force. Let us look at the legislation itself. Before reading this clause I shall repeat what I said two years ago and on several other occasions. It is perhaps reasonable that there should be some modification or change of this legislation. I told my hon. friend the Minister of Justice two years ago, and I tell him again to-night, that as far as I am concerned I should be quite willing to sit down with him and study certain amendments to this legislation; but I am opposed to repealing it en bloc. Let us consider the real point in the legislation. Section 98, subsection 1, of the criminal code, which it is sought to repeal by this bill, reads as follows:
Any association, organization, society or corporation, whose professed purpose or one of whose purposes is to bring about any governmental, industrial or economic change within Canada by use of force, violence or physical injury to person or property, or by threats of such injury, or which teaches, advocates, advises or defends the use of force, violence, terrorism, or physical injury to person or property. or threats of such injury, in order to accomplish such change, or for any other purpose, or which shall by any means prosecute or pursue such purpose or professed purpose, or shall so teach, advocate, advise or defend, shall be an unlawful association.
I submit to hon. members that such a measure ought to be on the statute book after the experience we have had in several sections of
the country. The first principle of any government is to offer security to life and property within the state. One of the first things an unorganized group of individuals would be called upon to do would be to organize themselves and to appoint some of their numbei to exercise this power. So- the clause simply declares illegal any group of persons who desire by force, violence or physical injury to person or property to undermine the authority of government. I submit that we have no right to remove a clause of that kind from the statute book. I am free to admit that in the subsequent clauses it may be that there are some points upon which there could be a disagreement of view, and the repeal or change or modification of which we might justly consider. I have no objection to approaching it in that way, but I do object to the real point of this legislation being tampered with.
Now, I have said this and much more on previous occasions, and I do feel that it is entirely wrong for my hon. friend to rise in his place and single out the Conservative party, intimating that they have in some invidious way secured the passage of legislation that is inimical to the welfare of any number of citizens of this country.
It is a compliment to be singled out like that.

Possibly. I repeat that the legislation was passed after -being carefully drafted, and personally I hope that the amendment fails. Unfortunately it is pretty clear that the committee will carry it, but there should be no reflections cast on those who may not agree with the majority decision.

The hon. gentleman has said that this bill was put through the house with great rapidity. I find that on May 1 1919, the then Solicitor General, the Hon Hugh Guthrie, moved:
That Messrs. Guthrie, Tweedie, McIntosh, Allan, Thomson, Boys, Douglas, Jacobs, Murphy, Ross, Archambault and Copp, be appointed a special committee to consider and report upon the law relating to sedition and seditious propaganda, and on any changes in the law which may be considered necessary to meet the existing conditions, and that the said committee have power to sit while the house is in session.
Mr. Speaker said:
This motion can only be entertained by unanimous consent.
And the house gave its consent, Mr. Guthrie having stated that in England a committee had been appointed to consider the English law upon the subject. I find that on June 10-not twenty minutes, but six weeks later-Mr. Guthrie at the opening of the
Criminal Code Amendment

house moved the adoption of the report of the committee. He set out the facts and law at some 'length, and I find in the course of his observations he said:
At the same time the greatest care will have to he exercised that there be no unnecessary interference with, nor curtailment of the sacred right of free speech.
Mr. Ernest Lapointe, whom I take to be the same hon. gentleman who is now Minister of Justice, said "hear, hear," and Mr. Guthrie concluded his remarks, indicating what the findings of the committee were. Whereupon the Hon. Charles Murphy said that there seemed to be a very earnest desire on the part of members to protect the rights of labour unions. He added:
Judging by the manner in which the house received the hon. gentleman's reference to the subject of free speech and the rights of organized labour, I take it that there is, at the present time, in any event, a unanimous opinion in this house that free speech and the rights of organized labour should not be interfered with. However that may be, such was the opinion that prevailed in the committee of which I was a member, and the report from which- not from the whole of which, however,-is now before the house.
Then he said:
There was in the committee a very sharp division of opinion as to the necessity of amending the criminal code, and there was a further division of opinion whether, in the event of the committee being of opinion that the criminal code with reference to sedition and seditious propaganda should be amended-in view of the numerous strikes and the general unrest throughout the country-this was the proper time to make such a report to the house and to induce a discussion of matters that would inevitably be discussed by reason of that report and of any action that might follow the introduction of that report.
He concluded his observations by saying that the minority report was not brought in, nor did they propose to move in that direction. He reserved anything further he might have to say on the subject until a future occasion, if the report of the committee should be concurred in and legislation based upon it introduced in the house. "Motion agreed to and report concurred in."
I have not before me the Hansard in which there appeared the report of the introduction of the bill, but that is the report on which the bill was based, a report unanimously concurred in, to which no amendment was moved The committee was moved on the first of May and the report brought down on June 10. So much for the hon. gentleman's accuracy with respect to the report.
How long did it take the bill to go through the house?

The point is that the bill was not based upon anyone's caprice. It was a bill reported by a committee that took six weeks to consider it. It was not a bill that originated in the mind of the Acting Prime Minister. I was not a member of that parliament, but I know that it was not one of those bills which are brought before the house suddenly in a panic. On the contrary, it was a bill which in terms was considered by a very select committee of the house, a representative committee on which there were eminent lawyers and laymen as well. As 1 say, they made their report on June 10, the committee having been appointed on May first.
Under these circumstances, I am sure, the hon. gentleman will desire to withdraw the observations he made as to the panicky character of this legislation. As to the bill, I have not been able to put my hand on the Hansard reporting its introduction, but I have sent for it and if I have an opportunity later on I shall direct the attention of the house to it. The fact is that the bill did pass through the house in a very short time. Why? Because a committee had spent all the time dealing with it and had given it very thorough consideration. Indeed, it was based upon a report which received far more consideration, far more time and attention, than have been devoted to any legislation passing through this house this session. At that time apprehension was expressed whether the language employed was sufficiently clear to protect the interests of trade unions, and since that time on many occasions it has been pointed out that it is capable oi being construed in a manner which would be injurious to those interests. But no case has arisen in which this fear is justified. The fact that the legislation stands in the form in which it is, after having been considered for weeks by a very representative committee, and the further fact that no cases have arisen under it that have impinged upon the rights of these unions, such as the Solicitor General had in mind when he made his motion to adopt the report of the committee, is in itself some evidence that if for a period of ten years that condition has prevailed, the same condition may be expected in the next ten years. The purposes for which the legislation was enacted are the purposes indicated in the report and in the speech of the Solicitor General. It is legislation which is intended to protect the people of this country, if occasion should arise. That is what most penal legislation is for. Under the circumstances I cannot see why the course

Criminal Code Amendment
taken by the Minister of Justice should not have been the proper course, of amending the legislation to meet any doubt which there might be that, as the Hon. Mr. Murphy pointed out at that time, the interests of the labour unions might be impaired and their rights impinged upon so far as free speech was concerned. Not having been in the house and not being therefore quite familiar with the matter, I have ventured to send for the Hansard report and I shall quote from it. I see that my friend the Minister of Justice has the report.

Quite so. A committee was appointed for the purpose of studying and considering the laws concerning sedition. Apparently this committee reported, and when the report was presented to the house Mr. Murphy, who was a member of the committee, said:

Mr. BENNE1T: The discussion would.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Murphy proved a
prophet. He went on:
The others who remained until the conclusion of the sitting did not submit a minority report, for the reason that they wished to avoid the very discussion which has been evoked here this afternoon, and such further discussion as may take place. Having informed the house of the division of opinion that prevailed in the committee, and as to the points on which that division of opinion existed, I shall reserve anything further I may have to say on the subject until a future occasion, if the report of the committee is concurred in and legislation based upon it is introduced in the house.
The motion was agreed to and the bill was introduced subsequently and passed the house in a very short time. My hon. friend from Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) seems to think that if this section disappears from the criminal code there will be nothing to protect society against sedition. That is absolutely wrong. If my hon. friend reads the speech of the Solicitor General of that day, the present member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie), he will see that the committee thought this might 'be a wise addition to the
provisions of the criminal code. The code provides for the punishment of sedition, and the common law applies to everything that may be considered seditious. The laws of the country as they stood at the time were sufficient, but it was thought by the committee that it might be advisable to have this special section added. As I have said, however, this section has never been invoked; it has never served any purpose whatever except to irritate the labour people of Canada and to give them a grievance, inasmuch as they think it is specially directed against the activities of their union. W'e do not think that it is necessary to keep this section in the criminal code. I agree with the decision of the British parliament and of the Canadian parliament as well, both of which take the view that the common law is sufficient in matters of sedition, and that it is not advisable to adopt in that respect the report of the commissioners who were entrusted with the task of codifying the criminal code, both in England and in this country. Parliament, after a long discussion, took the attitude that the common law was better than any section which might be added by the commissioners. I do not think myself that parliament in 1919 was as wise as that parliament which at a prior date decided not to change the provisions of the common law in this regard.

I am not blaming the members of the house for acting as they did; probably they acted according to the information Which they possessed, but I am inclined to think that some of us who were a little nearer to the scene of action had a more intimate knowledge of what was going on. I am inclined to think that if there was too great exuberance on the part of labour, there was also a certain panic on the part of other people, and I also believe that if labour exercised any governmental authority, some of the business men's organizations exercised governmental authority to a much greater extent. Mr. Speaker, as one who has persistently opposed the repeal of this legislation, and since my hon. friend has not been more specific in stating to whom he refers, I must necessarily consider that he refers to me at least in part.
I made no reference to the hon. gentleman.

I have persistently resisted the repeal of this legislation, perhaps more than anyone else, and I have done so for the reason which I intimated a moment ago. I believe that any persons who by force, violence or physical injury and so on seek to undermine or disturb the foundations of government in this country merit criminal action being taken against them. That is my point, and I do not care -whether they are labourites, capitalists, industrialists, farmers or any one

else. From that position I will not retire. On the other hand, I resent the suggestion of my hon. friend, who claims to speak for lalbour in Canada, that in taking the position we do we are branding labour as being more seditious than others. I have been in intimate touch with labour much longer, I think, than he has; I know the feeling and the heart of labour throughout this country just as thoroughly as he does, and I have the greatest sympathy with them.
They have asked to have this .rescinded.

Labour organizations may have, but I do not know that labour does. My hon. friend speaks with too much assurance. He refers to brief extracts from a speech made by a gentleman in Winnipeg. I do not know that I agree with the gentleman, but his language referring to a successful revolution referred to King John, who, it may be recalled, was guilty of a wholesale violation of the principles of government of the country over which he was king. The preamble of the very Magna Charta to which he refers states that this is a recital of the ancient rights and usages of the people, and they forced John to recognize that. In regard to King Charles whose head was cut off, 'he was guilty of imposing taxation-this was his chief offence- without the consent of parliament or of the people.
Supposing Charles had been successful, what would have happened then?

I am saying that the gentleman whose remarks were quoted-and his' language was rather loose-referred to well-known incidents in history. Later the same gentleman used this language, which is enlightening:
"England", he continued, "is not only a land of glory in the past, but a land of hope in the future, and Englishmen's ability to cope with an emergency, such as the general strike, leaves no room for doubt that they can cope with any emergency which may arise."
There was no emergency on the occasion of the strike in Great Britain.

But they passed legislation very much the same as that which we passed, and it is still upon the statute books of England. That legislation, found necessary with reference to conditions which then existed, was not dissimilar, I say, to the legislation to which we refer.

Still they are asking for

ganized labour in England, has repudiated the extremist and the revolutionary element in their party. And the Conservative party
as a result is going out of business.

May I ask the
speaker whether under the old czarist regime the people had not been persistently denied the right to govern, to have a Duma and so on?

Nobody who knows anything about history denies that. But what I say is that it has been demonstrated the world over, in the history of every country, the history of Rome, the history of almost every great empire, that revolution by force is not the expression of the will of the people but simply the seizure of power by well-organized minority groups. That is exactly what occurred in Winnipeg, where a small well-organized group of revolutionaries seized the power of government. They attempted the same thing in Vancouver and they failed, but in Seattle and Winnipeg they succeeded for a short time. In the city of Seattle they exercised absolute power for some three days, and it was only when they were driven out by force that they gave up the struggle.
It is a good thing the hon. member for Vancouver Centre does not represent Winnipeg, or he would learn what the citizens at large think about his statement.
I am not concerned with what they or anyone else think about it, nor with what they say.
It is not so much what they think of the statement itself as of the accuracy of it.
I am not concerned with what they think of the accuracy of it.
Is the hon. member not concerned about the accuracy of his statement?

I know it is accurate. The very gentlemen with whom my hon. friends are associated, a mere handful, improperly assumed that power, not by the use of the ballot, not with the concurrence of

Criminal Code Amendment
the majority of the people or any opportunity for them to say whether they wanted it or not; they amply seized and exercised power by force and imposed themselves upon the people. They attempted the same thing in the city of Vancouver, where they tied up some works for about ten days, but they made an utter fiasco of the affair. Why? Because the citizens of Vancouver as a whole repudiated and resisted the movement.
Just the same as they did in Winnipeg.

Just the same. Again I say to the Minister of Justice and to the government that I resist the repeal of this legislation in so far as it deals with this type of violence. I think this legislation ought to be on the statute book. I am willing to sit in with anybody in order to scan the legislation carefully, because there may be in it certain passages or clauses which might properly be repealed, modified or changed-and I admit I cited them, I think, two years ago when this question was before the house. But I am opposed to abandoning the principle of the legislation.

Mr. Speaker, I want to say a word in this most extraordinary debate. It seems to be a debate between the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Voodsworth) as to whether the Conservative party or the Labour party is the least revolutionary. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre assures us that the Labour party is not revolutionary, not nearly as revolutionary as certain lawyers in Winnipeg. That comes to me as a great surprise. I imagine, if we analyse the revolutions of history, we shall discover that they came just as epidemics of typhoid might come.
From bad water.

Yes, from bad water.
Typhoid comes from bad water and bad sewage. Similarly revolution comes when there is bad government, economic or social or political oppression, and no law placed on the statute books of any country in the world will prevent a revolution arising if the necessary oppression or the condition which breeds revolution is produced. When you come to look at the matter in that regard, I imagine the labour people of any country are far more likely to be revolutionary than the bankers' association. The bankers' association are perfectly satisfied with the present system and conditions because they are getting their bread buttered on both sides. But When
the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre tells us that the labour people are less revolutionary than the bankers' association, I am glad to know that because it means that conditions for labour in Canada must be excellent..
That is all I wish to say, beyond this one thing: that the legislation under discussion is in my opinion of the nature of oppression. I do not doubt the sincerity of the people who placed it on the statute book. The hon. gentlemen who were responsible for the legislation were responsible for the government of the country at that time. I have no criticism to offer in that respect, but I believe the legislation itself is of the nature of oppression and that it would do more towards bringing about than preventing a revolution.

Mr. Speaker, before this discussion closes I wish to add a word. The legislation we are repealing I have never considered necessary, and I deem it superfluous in any country where democracy is practised without partiality. In its essence legislation of this kind carries with it the implication of lawlessness on the part of some class or other. Whom does it implicate in this case? It implicates a class who have been under the domination of some other class and who have realized their helplessness to exact a square deal in any other way than by revolution. Parliament has a sovereign power to enforce law; but we may well ask: what is law? Law is the juridical sanction which is given to the will of the ruling class or the class which happens to be in power at the time. I believe the juridical sanction has been given for many years by parliament to laws which have been unjust to the workers and primary producers.
I say again that the sovereign power of parliament has been used for many years to enforce the juridical sanction of a code of legislation in accordance with the will of a powerful political-commercial or political-financial group in this house. I was amazed, nay, I was startled by the words of the leader of the opposition on one occasion since I came to parliament, and that was when we sent the soldiers presumably to enforce law in Nova Scotia but in reality to protect the so-considered rights and property of a tyrannical body which was oppressing its men. The leader of the opposition upbraided the Minister of Militia across the floor of this house in 1923 and said: "You have gathered up the militia all the way from Winnipeg and sent them east, and now what protection has western Canada?" There was trouble at Powell River at that time. I understand.
Criminal Code Amendment

Mr. Speaker, that we were then relying on force in this house rather than a square deal to preserve the peace and good government of this country. In the last few years we have tyrannically applied this force to our own shame, I say, and Canada may well be ashamed of the extent to which we have applied that force. Legislation of this kind will be needed so long as parliament as a body fails to protect the rights of the workers and the primary producers. Wage earners and labourers never strike until they realize their helplessness in getting a square deal by other means, and revolution has never taken place in any country except under those conditions.
My hon. friend has mentioned Russia. Russia is an exact case in point where the workers of a country have risen in their might because of untoward conditions under which they have been compelled to labour. It is within mjr own memory when conditions prevailed in that country under which no human being could live in any respectable way. I can remember when an order was issued by the czar himself, because of the condition of the peasants who occupied the land in that country, permitting them to go into the forests and pick up the dry branches that had fallen that they might use them for fuel, and gather up the fallen leaves for fodder. That was the condition which prevailed for many years in that country, and when at last the people rose we raised our hands in horror and called them bolshevik and Red. But revolutions never occur in any country until the people realize their helplessness to obtain a square deal ip any other way. It is for parliament, therefore, and the country to study these conditions, to examine with care the road we are travelling, and, if all is not right, to take whatever steps may be necessary in the light of justice and reason.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition) :
speechtext:
But for the observations that were made to-night by the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) as to the circumstances under which this measure was originally passed, I should not on the third reading of the bill make any further observations. The hon. gentleman says that this bill was passed in 1919 as the result of a sudden panic, and after only twenty minutes consideration. My memory was not quite that, although I was not in the house at the time, and so I ventured to send to the library and get Hansard. The record shows that on the 1st day of May, 1919, a committee of this house under the chairmanship of the then Solicitor General, the Hon.

Hugh Guthrie, was appointed to consider the whole question with respect to sedition. Upon that committee there were many members of the Liberal party, the Union government then being in power.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There were very few
Liberals in the house at that time.
But the present Minister of Justice was one.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Not on the committee.

No, not on the committee, but the Hon. Charles Murphy was on the committee, as well as Mr. Copp, the exSecretary of State. That committee made a report, but not until the 10th day of June. Their findings were not unanimous, but they made no minority report; no amendment was moved, and the report was unanimously adopted by the House of Commons. Then what happened? On the 27th of Jun,e, seventeen days after the report had been made and adopted, the Hon. Arthur Meighen, Acting Minister of Justice, moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 160, to amend the crim-minal code. Mr. McKenzie, then leading the Liberal party, asked him to explain, and Mr. Meighen made half a column of explanation. Mr. Murphy stated what his position had been, and then at page 4135 of Hansard, the motion is stated to have been agreed to and the bill read the first time.
I find that the bill was read the second time on the 1st of July. Page 4355 of Hansard shows that on motion of the Hon. Arthur Meighen, then Acting Minister of Justice, bill No. 160, to amend the criminal code, was read the second time and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Boivin in the chair. Mr. Meighen explained that the bill was taken from the report of the committee except with a slight variation with respect to justice, instead of justices, of the peace. Then there followed a discussion in which Mr. Jacobs and Mr. McMaster participated, and finally, Mr. Meighen having made further explanations, Mr. Guthrie having made some, and Mr. Bureau having participated in the debate, we find that the bill was adopted. It was not, however, given its third reading that day.
Did the hon. gentleman state that the bill was read on the 6th day of June? Were there not two different bills?

I did not say anything about the 6th of June. I said that the committee was appointed on the 1st of May, that on the 10th of June it made its report, that on the 27th of June a bill based on the report

Criminal Code Amendment
of the committee was introduced and given a first reading, and that on the 1st of July the bill was given its second reading. There was not any twenty minutes hurry to get it through and read a third time that day, because according to Hansard, page 4380, on motion of the Hon. Arthur IMeighen, Acting Minister of Justice, Bill No. 160, to amend the criminal code, was read the third time and passed, the date being the 2nd day of July. That is, between the 1st of May, when the committee was first appointed, and the 2nd day of July, when the bill received its third reading and was passed, not on division, but without a question being raised against it, a period of two months had elapsed-not twenty minutes.

Does the hon. gentleman
state that that bill amending the criminal code had reference to sedition, to what we are dealing with here?

Surely. This is the very bill we are talking about. Now, we go a step further. The bill could not become law until it had gone to the senate. On the 5th of July the bill came back from the senate, and page 4660 of Hansard shows that the house proceeded to the consideration of amendments made by the senate to Bill No. 160, to amend the criminal code. Mr. Meighen explained the differences between the amendments made by the senate and the bill as it left the House of Commons, and then at page 4661 of Ha-sard, we find these words:

Motion agreed to, and concurred in.
The motion being that the senate amendments be concurred in. The bill did not then become law; it had to receive the royal assent. The royal assent was given to the bill when the house prorogued on the 7th of July, 1919.
It is just such statements, Mr. Speaker, as were made by the hon. member for North Winnipeg to-night that are responsible for the conditions aimed at by this legislation. I have no doubt that he has endeavoured to inflame the minds of labour men by inducing them to believe that this parliament did something in twenty minutes which it should have taken them two months to do, and which this parliament actually took over two months to do. It is just as the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) has pointed out:	you
arouse the animosities and prejudices and suspicions of groups of men by intimating that this parliament, reflecting the mind of plutocrats and others, has been endeavouring to crush free speech amongst the labour men of the country, when the very report made by the committee and! the Observations of those in charge of the legislation show that the facts
were directly the opposite. I join with my friend from Vancouver Centre in stating that in all this country there is no group of men more desirous of the enforcement of law and order than those organized under labour unions, for their very freedom of speech and continuance in useful existence depends upon their having the unfailing support of law and order. They must have order that they may pursue their vocations; they must have the protection of the law because under our institutions every man stands on an equality before the law: they must have those things if they are to prosper and maintain their families.
When the hon. member for Rosetown (Mr. Evans) referred to what took place in 1923 as to the raising of troops, I wondered if he had reference to observations I had made as leader of the opposition. I had no memory of having done so. I was not sitting in the house at that time, but I doubt not it will be found that the then leader of the opposition by his observations intended to ensure peace, order, good government, prosperity, happiness -all of which spring from a just and proper observance of law and recognition of the equality of every man under the law. That is the important thing to remember-the equality of all men under the law, rich or poor, high or low. In this country so far, despite the attempts made at times to induce people to believe that it is otherwise, I have seen no instance in which I could not say truly that I believe in the administration of our criminal law every man stands on an equal footing-something which does not obtain in certain other countries.
I have never seen a more striking illustration than that afforded by the observations of the hon. member for North Winnipeg in his attempt to have the house believe that in a moment of panic parliament rushed through in twenty minutes this legislation that is now being repealed. I believed it until I found that over two months elapsed from the time the motion was made for the appointment of the special committee until it made its report on the 10th of June and the bill was finally passed into law early in July. It is just such statements as that which arouse and inflame the minds of those who look to the member for North Winnipeg and others for leadership. .Instead of accurate statements they receive misstatements, which lead them into conditions that imperil their liberty and bring discredit upon their organizations. That is the position we have before us to-night. That is why upon the third reading of this bill I have taken the trouble to direct the

Traffic in Intoxicating Liquors
attention of the house to every stage of the measure from the time the special committee was appointed until the bill received the royal assent. Had it not been that I sent to the library for Hansard, the statement would have gone on record that this bill, supposedly a panic measure, was passed in twenty minutes by parliament because it was believed there was red revolution in the streets of Winnipeg. That was not the fact.
I do not propose further to trespass on the time of the house, but I conceive it to be a public duty to frown down any effort made to induce large bodies of our people to believe that this is the way parliament acts. This is what arouses unrest and hatred, instead of peace, unity and high desire to promote the interests of one another that usually characterize Canadian citizens whether they be found in parliament or elsewhere. I resent any effort to mislead the people in the way to which I have alluded.
Motion agreed to, and bill read the third
time and passed.

Hon. ERNEST LAPOINTE (Minister of Justice) moved the second reading of Bill No. 192, respecting interprovincial and international traffic in intoxicating liquors.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Johnston in the chair.
On section 1-Short title.

I congratulate the Minister of Justice on bringing forward this legislation. The provinces have long sought it. It will enable them beyond question to make effective their legislation, removing any doubt of the constitutionality of the statutes passed by the various provinces that have dealt with the liquor problem through government control. That is what is intended I understand, although the Nadan decision cleared the air.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes; and it applies to two provinces which did not come under the old law.

Section agreed to.
Section 2 agreed to.
On section 3-Importation into province forbidden, etc.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I have two amendments to offer to section 3. First, by inserting after the word "railway" in the third line of paragraph (a) of subsection (2), the words:
including any necessary transfer by truck or railway car to a ship, or vice versa,
The subsection will then read:
The provisions of subsection one of this section shall not apply to
(a)	the carriage or transportation of intoxicating liquor into and through a province by means only of a common carrier by water or by railway, including any necessary transfer by truck or railway car to a ship, or vice versa, if. during the time the intoxicating liquor is being so carried or transported, the package or vessel containing the intoxicating liquor is not opened or broken or any of the intoxicating liquor drunk or used therefrom.
This is to cover cases where the railway has to transfer the liquor to a ship.
Where there are no interchange facilities.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Yes. The other amendment is to add a new subsection to section 3, as follows:
The transfer from one distillery to another of any spirits or liquor which is permitted by any act or regulation lawfully in force, or by special permit of the Department of National Revenue.
This is suggested by the Department of National Revenue.

Amendments agreed to.
Section as amended agreed to.
Sections 4 and 5 agreed to.
On section 6-Prosecution in place where liquor imported.

Is it the intention of the department to leave the enforcement of this provision entirely to the provincial officials, or does the Dominion government intend to assume some responsibility? I notice here that no prosecution can be entered without the consent of the attorney general of the province. In any case where there is complaint in Manitoba, say, in regard to liquor being shipped into that province from Saskatchewan, I presume the Manitoba police will be empowered to deal with those who receive liquor in Manitoba. But the punishment of those shipping the liquor will evidently be left to the other province. It seems to me it would be difficult in these cases to get the provincial authorities to act. The logical thing would be for the federal authorities to take the responsibility.
Immigration Act

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The same provision appeared in part IV of the Canada Temperance Act, which had the effect of supplementing the legislation of every province in regard to the prevention of liquor importations, and the provinces themselves have asked that this provision should be made, I do not think there will be any difficulty.

It seems to me that this is only one step in the direction of the objective we all have in view, namely, the better enforcement of the liquor laws. Where there are such enormous profits as in the liquor business you will always have great difficulty in enforcing the law, and now that nearly all the provinces have public control of the sale of liquor, it would be only logical for the Dominion government to nationalize the manufacture of liquor. This may seem rather drastic, but I have in mind bringing before this parliament next session a resolution on this question.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Does the hon. member suggest that we engage in the trade of distillers?

Yes; nationalize the
manufacture. If you did that you would not increase the evil any more than the provincial governments to-day are increasing the evil by selling liquor, and you would curtail to a considerable extent the lawlessness which now surrounds the whole traffic. Anyone who has read the report of the royal commission that recently examined into the action of the brewers will be impressed with the fact that it is almost impossible for the authorities to enforce the law. What with the falsification of reports, and the illegal shipment of liquor here and there, the authorities are powerless to deal with the situation. I know the Minister of Justice and other members of the government will hesitate to take a step so drastic as nationalizing the breweries, but it is my conviction that this is the only way you will ever get to the root of the evil.

Section agreed to.
