Hon. ROBERT FORKE (Minister of Immigration and Colonization) moved the second reading of Bill No. 187, to amend the Immigration Act.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Johnston in the chair.
On section 1-Persons deemed to belong to prohibited classes.

This bill is designed to
make deportation for certain causes dependent upon conviction in Canada under part II of the criminal code relating to offences against public order, rather than upon a bearing before a board of inquiry condemning certain offences under section 41 of the Immigration
Immigration Act

Act. Proceedings for the deportation of such undesirable classes are provided by sections 40, 42 and 43 of the act, and under these sections deportation may be carried out. It is considered that the provisions of section 41 are unnecessary, as section 40 and part II of the criminal code cover the case. Section 41 of the Immigration act reads:
Every person who
(a)	by word or act in Canada seeks to overthrow by force or violence the government of or constituted law and authority in the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, or Canada, or any of the provinces of Canada, or the government of any other pf His Majesty's dominions, colonies, possessions or dependencies, or advocates the assassination of any official of any of the said governments or of any foreign government, or who in Canada defends or suggests the unlawful destruction of property or by word or act creates or attempts to create any riot or public disorder in Canada; or
(b)	without lawful authority assumes any powers of government in Canada or in any part thereof; or
(c)	by common repute belongs to or is suspected of belonging any secret society or organization which extorts money from or in anyway attempts to control any resident of Canada by force or by threat of bodily harm, or by blackmail; or
(d)	is a member of or affiliated with any
organization entertaining or teaching disbelief in or opposition to organized government; shall, for the purposes of this act, be deemed to belong to the prohibited or undesirable classes, and shall be liable to deportation in the manner provided by this act, and it shall be the duty of any officer becoming cognizant thereof and of the clerk, secretary or other official of any municipality in Canada wherein any such person may be, forthwith to send a written complaint to the minister, giving full particulars:	Provided, that this section shall not
apply to any person who is a British subject, either by reason of birth in Canada, or by reason of naturalization in Canada.
This amendment to the Immigration Act has been before the house four times, I believe, and has been adopted each time. I might point out that the crimes or misdemeanors mentioned in this section are pretty well taken care of by the criminal code and also by section 3, subsection (n) and (o) of the Immigration Act. Those sections refer particularly to immigrants newly coming to Canada who are dealt with at the port of debarkation. This matter has been debated in this house so often that I believe every hon. member is pretty well aware of the arguments which can be advanced for and against the amendment. You will notice that this does not apply to anyone who is a British subject by reason of birth or naturalization in Canada. It means that under this section no immigrant coming from England, no matter how long he may have been in Canada, can claim a trial by a judge and jury for
[Mr. Forked
treason or any of the misdemeanors mentioned; no matter how long he may have been in Canada he is still liable to deportation. When the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre mentioned Mr. Jackson Dodds, who is a very estimable and highly respected citizen of Winnipeg, it just struck me that he would come under this section and would be liable to deportation should he be found guilty of using any language which might be thought treasonable.
He only presided at the banquet; Mr. Graham used the language.

That is so, but it did strike me that if Mr. Dodds had made those statements he would have been liable for deportation if the circumstances corresponded to those which existed at the time this section was placed in the Immigration Act.
I think this amendment should appeal to the sense of fair play of all the members of this house. British immigrants have been treated so well and so generously by native-born Canadians that I think as a matter of fair play they should be treated in this regard as well as we treat an immigrant coming from Central Europe. Just the other evening the hon. member for Comox-Albemi brought a lady to my room in a very indignant frame of mind. She had resided in Canada for sixteen years, and upon going home for a visit to England had overstayed the one year period during which British immigrants may remain abroad without notice to the Department of Immigration. When an immigrant overstays that limit he loses his domicile and can only return to Canada as an immigrant. That is another thing that I would like to see remedied. This lady found herself in that position, and she was very indignant that she, a good citizen of British Columbia, should be treated as an immigrant when she wanted to return to Canada. She also told me it was quite common talk in her locality in England that if a British immigrant came to Canada and committed any crime, immediately he would be deported back to England no matter how long he had stayed in this country. I know this is entirely wrong; that only applies where certain crimes have been committed, but hon. gentlemen will appreciate the effect such a story might have. I hear a great deal these days about the Department of Immigration not being as anxious as it should be to secure British immigrants.
Mr. BENNETT; Hear, hear.
Mr. FORKE; The leader of the opposition says "hear, hear;" I hope he does not think

Immigration Act
the Minister of Immigration is guilty of that fault. However, hon. members will quite appreciate that a rumour of that kind will have its effect upon English people who may desire to come to Canada. This lady said she had been in Canada sixteen years; she was a good Canadian; this was her country, and she could not understand any law which would make a distinction between her and a native born Canadian. An alien coming from continental Europe enjoys privileges that are not enjoyed by British subjects.
The name of Hon. D. D. McKenzie has been mentioned to-night, but I do not think I can agree with what the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre said about that gentleman. I remember a conversation which I had with him a number of years ago, with regard to this section of the Immigration Act; while I did not feel very strongly about it I thought it rather cast a reflection upon British immigrants. I remember that Mr. McKenzie, in his inimitable way, said to me, "Oh, don't be afraid, Mr. Forke; we will never deport you." In that sentence he put me in an entirely different class from native-born Canadians; and I think that is the real difficulty. It is largely a matter of sentiment, because I do not believe it likely that any reputable citizen coming to Canada from Great Britain and living in this country will be deported; but sentiment, Mr. Chairman, is a very powerful thing and has very great influence. The act as it stands puts it in the hands of the minister or his officers, without trial, to deport anyone on mere suspicion of sedition. That is to say, a board of inquiry of the immigration officials can deport anyone who is suspected of treason, without trial. As a matter of fair play I think anyone who has come to Canada, who has been a good citizen, who has lived here for years, who has done his part in the developing of the country, participated in its interests and activities, is at least entitled to trial by a judge and jury, and then if found guilty he may be deported to the country from which he came.
I do not know that it is necessary to make any lengthy speech on this subject. It is perfectly evident what is involved in the elimination of this section from the Immigration Act. I would appeal to the hon. members on the other side to look upon this matter in a broad way-I will not say in a charitable way, but from a sense of even-handed justice. I know that no hon. member on that side wishes to cast any slur upon immigrants from Great Britain, but it does seem peculiar that a man can come to Canada and marry a Canadian girl, and his children will have
privileges which he does not enjoy. The sense of fair play in the thing appeals to me, and I ask that this section be taken out of the Immigration Act.
Mr. McQUARRlE:	How many men or
women have been deported under this provision?

I do not know that any have been deported, but it oasts a stigma upon men and women who may have been in this country for forty years, and who are in this respect not on an equality with those who have come here and have received Canadian citizenship. It is not a matter of suffering, but it is a matter of sentiment; and sentiment is sometimes stronger than law. I am not making any complaint. I have every reason to be thankful and proud of the privileges which I have enjoyed as a British immigrant, and I have found the Canadian people warmhearted and ready to extend to all British immigrants kind treatment. I would appeal to the' house to remove this stigma, because it is a stigma on British immigrants.

The minister has referred to one matter which I think should engage the attention of parliament, and when this bill is before the house it should possibly be determined by an amendment. He referred to a lady who had lived in Canada for some sixteen years, but who, having been absent in Great Britain on a visit, when she came back to this country found that she was treated as an immigrant.

Because she had been in
England more than a year.

Let me state what I
conceive the law would be. The domicile of a person is not necessarily (his residence. Domicile consists of two factors, namely, the anima, the state of mind or intention-I will not use the legal word-of the person, plus the fact of residence. Any person who comes into Canada from any other country with the intention of making this country his or her home, and who resides here for even a short time, is in law domiciled in Canada. So that when this lady went to England and stayed there for fifteen or eighteen months, the question as to what her intentions were would become of paramount importance. If her intention was still to make her home in Canada, when she came back to resume her residence in the country that she had chosen as her home by intention, her domicile was still Canadian.
24S6
Immigration Act

If she had declared her
intention of returning to Canada.

There is the difficulty.
The question has frequently engaged the attention of the courts, in connection with succession duties. An outstanding case is the Widmer case. A very rich American who bad for many years resided in Great Britain, and had very large sums of money in the Bank of England, died, and his estate was taxed for succession duty by the British authorities. It was contended that he had never lost his domicile. The decision ultimately was that there was no evidence to show that he had ever expressed an intention to make England his permanent home, although he had resided there. There was no such expression of intention as would indicate the two factors had combined, namely, the intention to make his home in England, and the residence in pursuance of his intention. His property in Great Britain therefore, was not taxable as though he were a domiciled Englishman. I contend that our statute should be changed; we should say that any person domiciled in Canada may return to Canada at any time. For why should a domiciled Canadian be shut out of this country? My hon. friend from Battle River (Mr. Spencer) I daresay has in mind the case of one of his constituents, a man from England who went over to England and lived there, and then found he could not get back into Canada because in the meantime he had suffered ill health and was not in perfect physical condition. I regard that as a very serious situation. The minister should consider whether there should not be an amendment added declaring clearly that a domiciled Canadian cannot be kept out of Canada. If the Minister of Railways and Canals were to go to England for fifteen months and then come back, the Minister of Immigration would have to issue a permit for him to enter Canada. My friend from Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) would be in exactly the same position.
Worse than that, both of us can be deported without trial.

I have no doubt that if
the hon. gentleman spoke his mind they both would be deported.
Progress reported.
